text:
In 1975, Steve Jobs told Steve Wozniak that Atari had paid them $700 for a game Wozniak built in four sleepless nights. He wrote Woz a check for $350.

Atari had actually paid Jobs $5,000.

In the video below, Wozniak explains why he would have let Jobs keep every dollar if he had just told the truth.

Jobs only had his job at Atari because of Wozniak in the first place. Woz had built a home version of Pong out of 28 $1 chips. Jobs carried the board into Atari's lobby, let them assume he had designed it, and got hired as a technician.

Because Jobs clashed with coworkers, Atari put him on the night shift alone.

Then Atari founder Nolan Bushnell asked for a single-player brick-breaking game, later named Breakout. Atari's engineers were using 150 to 190 chips per cabinet, so the company offered $700 plus a $100 bonus for every chip eliminated below 100.

Jobs couldn't design the circuit. He went to Wozniak, who worked days at Hewlett-Packard, told him they had four days, and promised to split the fee 50/50.

A hardware arcade board normally took six months. Wozniak designed it by day and wired it with Jobs at night, going four straight days without sleep. Both of them came down with mononucleosis.

Wozniak got the entire game down to 45 chips. The design was so tight that Atari's own engineers couldn't figure out how it worked to manufacture it.

Atari still paid Jobs the full $5,000 bonus. Jobs told Wozniak they got $700, handed him a check for $350, and used the other $4,650 to buy into an apple orchard commune in Oregon.

"He should have said, 'I need the money to buy into a farm in Oregon,' and I would say take it all," Wozniak says. "Who cares about money? Well, you do care about friendship and honesty."

There was an irony to those four sleepless nights. While sitting exhausted at his Atari workbench staring at a test TV, Wozniak figured out how to generate color digitally with a $1 chip instead of a $1,000 board. That breakthrough became the Apple II, the computer that made them both rich.

Wozniak didn't learn the real Breakout payout until nine years later, when he read it in a book about Atari on an airplane.

By then, the pattern was set. Before Apple's 1980 IPO, Jobs refused to give a single share to Daniel Kottke, his college friend who had hand-wired the first Apple prototypes in Jobs's garage.

Wozniak did the opposite. He sold $10 million of his own pre-IPO stock for pennies to 40 early employees Jobs had left out, and gave Kottke $500,000 in shares for free.

One partner pocketed $4,650 from his best friend. The other gave away $10 million to the people who built the company.

Was Jobs's ruthlessness the reason Apple won, or did Wozniak prove you didn't need to treat people that way to build a giant?

text:
Where were you the last time you approved a video ad for your business?

Probably at your desk or in a meeting, watching it full screen with the sound on, after you'd already read the script and sat through a couple rounds of edits. You knew the product, you knew the offer and you knew exactly what the ad was trying to say before the first frame even played.

That's a big problem, because the person you're actually trying to sell has none of that. They're on their phone, half paying attention, often with the sound off and they've probably never heard of you.

A famous study from Stanford shows how big that gap is. A grad student named Elizabeth Newton had people tap out the rhythm of well known songs on a table while someone else tried to guess the song. Before they started, the tappers predicted the listeners would get it right about half the time, but out of 120 songs the listeners only got 3.

The tappers were not bad at tapping. They just couldn't stop hearing the melody in their heads, so they couldn't imagine what it sounded like to someone who only heard knocking.

This is called the curse of knowledge and the basic idea is that once you know something it gets really hard to picture not knowing it. When you approve your own ads you're the tapper, because you hear the whole song every single time you watch it.

That's how ads get approved where the product doesn't show up until halfway through, the voiceover does all the selling with no words on screen, or the opening shot only makes sense if you already know what the company sells.

Here's how I'd change the way you review video ads:

1. Watch it on your phone in the feed preview with the sound off. If you can't tell what's being sold and why someone would want it without the audio, a lot of people scrolling past won't either.

2. Show it to someone who doesn't know your business (a friend, your spouse, someone on a different team) and ask them what it's for. Don't explain anything first, because the second you explain it you've turned them into a tapper too.

3. Pay attention to the first thing they say, not whether they liked it. "It's some kind of water bottle?" tells you way more than "looks great."

None of this replaces the numbers. An ad that passes this check still has to bring in customers at a cost that works and plenty of ads that look rough in a review end up being winners. But it'll catch the ads that only make sense to the people who made them before you spend real money finding that out.

text:
During Tuesday’s Google I/O keynote, Demis Hassabis, the CEO of Google DeepMind, proclaimed that we are currently “standing in the foothills of the singularity.” It was a striking statement—the singularity is the theoretical future moment when AI rapidly exceeds human intelligence and dramatically transforms the world. But what struck me as I listened in the audience was the context in which he said those words. 

He was on stage to close out the session with a segment on scientific AI, the centerpiece of which was a video detailing how the company’s weather prediction software provided an advance alert about Hurricane Melissa’s catastrophic landfall in Jamaica last year—and potentially saved lives. If that software, called WeatherNext, helped anyone escape the storm or better fortify their home, that’s an enormous and meaningful achievement. But it’s hardly evidence of an impending singularity.

The juxtaposition of Hassabis’s lofty rhetoric with the real-world results of WeatherNext highlighted the tension between two very different approaches to AI for science. The first focuses on AI tools, like WeatherNext, that are designed and trained to solve specific scientific problems. The second is agentic, LLM-based systems that could one day execute cutting-edge research projects without human involvement.

This second vision powers a great deal of AI enthusiasm right now, including recent excitement around recursive self-improvement, or the idea that AI systems could eventually become the primary drivers of AI advancement—a process that would get faster and faster as the AI systems grow smarter. And agentic systems are now making real research contributions, sometimes with limited human guidance.

Just this week, Pushmeet Kohli, Google Cloud’s chief scientist, published a piece in a special AI and science issue of the journal Daedalus, writing: “We are moving toward AI that doesn’t just facilitate science but begins to do science.” With autonomous AI scientists on the horizon, it’s harder to justify massive efforts to develop super-specialized tools—even one like AlphaFold, for which DeepMind scientists won a Nobel Prize, or a potentially life-saving system like WeatherNext. It also heralds a far stranger future for science, in which humans and AI systems collaborate as peers—or AI even makes scientific progress on its own.

To be clear, Google does not appear to be abandoning its work on specialized AI-for-science tools. AlphaGenome and AlphaEarth Foundations, which are trained for genetics and Earth science applications respectively, were released last summer, and the newest version of WeatherNext came out in November.

What’s more, such tools remain extremely popular among scientists. Last year, for instance, Google reported that protein structure predictions from AlphaFold have been used by over 3 million researchers worldwide. And Isomorphic Labs, a Google subsidiary that aims to use AlphaFold and related technologies to develop new drugs, just raised a $2 billion Series B funding round.

But there are concrete signs of realignment, in both enthusiasm and resources. Last month, the Los Angeles Times reported that Google fellow John Jumper, who won the Nobel for AlphaFold, is now working on AI coding, not on science-specific AI tools. It’s not surprising that Google is assigning its best minds to the coding problem, as the company has recently taken a reputational hit because its coding tools don’t currently stand up to those offered by Anthropic and OpenAI. But it may also signal a prioritization of agentic science on Google’s part, as coding abilities are key to the success of some of those systems. 

Across the industry, agentic researcher systems are showing real potential. This week, OpenAI announced that one of its models had disproved an important mathematics conjecture—perhaps the most meaningful contribution that generative AI has made to mathematics so far, according to some mathematicians.

Importantly, the model used by OpenAI is not specialized for solving mathematical problems, or even for research; according to the company, it’s a general-purpose reasoning model in the vein of GPT-5.5. If general agents can make independent contributions to mathematical research, they might soon be able to do the same in science (though the fact that ideas in science must be verified experimentally makes it a tougher domain for AI).

Google is certainly devoting a lot of attention to an agent-driven scientific future. The big scientific announcement at I/O was the new Gemini for Science package, which unites several of the company’s LLM-based scientific systems under one brand.

This includes the hypothesis-generating AI Co-Scientist and algorithm-optimizing AlphaEvolve, which are still not publicly available—but as Google is now allowing any researcher to apply for access to Gemini for Science, they may soon see wider adoption in the scientific community. Scientists who were involved in early testing are enthusiastic about their potential: Gary Peltz, a Stanford geneticist, compared using the AI Co-Scientist to “consulting the oracle of Delphi” in a Nature Medicine article.

Gemini for Science isn’t incompatible with specialized tools; to the contrary, agentic systems can be designed to call on such tools when they might be useful. And no agentic system can predict the structure that a protein will fold into without AlphaFold’s help (at least not yet). But the company seems to be shifting its public image—and at least some resources and personnel, such as Jumper—away from specifically developing those kinds of tools. Though it has only been five years since AlphaFold solved the protein-folding problem, both the technology and the discourse have quickly moved beyond that once-revolutionary achievement.

Google has been careful to position this new set of scientific agents as an accelerant for human scientists, rather than a replacement for them—the choice of the name AI Co-Scientist as opposed to AI Scientist, for instance, appears quite deliberate. Hassabis uses that same human-centric framing when he talks about changes in the landscape of scientific AI. “For the next decade or so, we should think about AI as this amazing tool to help scientists,” Hassabis said in an interview published in the Daedalus issue. “Beyond that timeframe, it is hard to say with any certainty, but perhaps these systems will become more like collaborators.”

But no one can be an effective scientific collaborator without also being a skilled scientist in their own right. And if Hassabis is anywhere near the mark when he talks about the “foothills of the singularity,” then AI scientists could eventually exceed the capabilities of their human counterparts.

In a discussion with the journalist Mike Allen at I/O, Hassabis spoke of how he was initially inspired to pursue AI when he observed how progress in physics had stagnated since the 1970s; he wondered whether the human mind had reached its limits in that domain, and if AI could help to overcome that barrier. Superhuman agentic scientists would certainly fit that bill. We might not ever get anywhere near there, but Google seems to be aiming itself toward that summit.

text:
During the Vietnam War, soldiers reported seeing nightmarish winged creatures through red-tinted night vision—were they hallucinations or something far more sinister?
Case File: The Red Night Vision Goggles and Winged Demons of Vietnam
Case No.: NV-1967-VN
Classification: Unexplained Military Phenomenon / Paranormal Sightings
Location: Dense jungles of Vietnam, various conflict zones
Date of Incident: 1967 to 1971
Filed by: US Military Personnel, Night Patrol Squads, Helicopter Gunners, and Unnamed Witnesses
Status: Closed – Equipment Replaced, Explanation Inconclusive
Incident Summary
During the Vietnam War, US forces deployed early-generation red-tinted infrared night vision goggles intended to give soldiers a tactical advantage in the dense jungle terrain. These devices provided visibility in the pitch-black conditions of the jungle, casting a reddish hue over everything seen through the goggles. However, soldiers using the goggles began reporting encounters with horrifying entities that appeared only through this red-tinted vision. Disturbing figures, shadowy shapes, and creatures with glowing eyes became recurring sights, sparking rumors of something supernatural lurking within the jungle.
In addition to these ground-level encounters, helicopter door gunners on night flights soon began reporting terrifying experiences of their own. During night missions, when visibility was low, gunners would occasionally open fire into the air, seemingly at random. When questioned, these gunners claimed to have seen massive winged creatures flying beside or even above the helicopters, describing them as “demons” or “dragons” with glowing eyes and leathery wings.
These unsettling encounters grew so frequent that the US military eventually replaced the red night vision goggles with green-tinted models, which offered superior clarity and did not produce the eerie red glow. After the switch, reports of these terrifying visions and winged creatures largely ceased. Despite this, stories of these encounters persisted among Vietnam veterans, becoming part of military lore and fueling speculation that the Vietnam War held a supernatural aspect.
Phenomena Overview
The following phenomena are commonly reported by soldiers who used the red-tinted infrared night vision goggles and helicopter gunners on night missions:

Shadowy Figures in the Jungle: Soldiers frequently reported seeing shadow-like figures moving through the trees, often described as humanoid but with elongated limbs or distorted shapes. These figures seemed to disappear if the soldiers removed the goggles or looked directly at them.
Glowing Eyes and Monstrous Forms: Many accounts describe glowing eyes that would appear in the distance, followed by brief sightings of large, grotesque figures. These beings were often described as having animalistic or monstrous features and sometimes appeared to hover or move with unnatural speed.

Feelings of Dread and Disembodied Whispers: Soldiers wearing the red goggles reported feeling a creeping sense of dread or sudden drops in temperature, accompanied by whispers or murmurs that could not be traced to any specific source.

Winged Demons in the Sky: Helicopter door gunners on night missions occasionally opened fire into the empty air, claiming to have seen enormous winged creatures flying alongside or above the helicopters. These creatures were described as having bat-like wings, long tails, and piercing eyes that glowed through the darkness.

Paralysis and Entrancement: Some soldiers reported feeling a paralyzing fear when encountering these entities, as though they were unable to look away or move. Others felt a bizarre compulsion to walk toward the creatures, despite their intense fear.

Investigation Overview

While the US military did not conduct an official investigation into these sightings, multiple unofficial reports and witness testimonies have been documented. Military psychologists were deployed to address troop morale and mental health, though no official acknowledgment of the supernatural aspects was made public.
Internal Reports (1967-1971): The US military initially dismissed the sightings as stress-induced hallucinations, attributing them to the extreme conditions of jungle warfare. However, the widespread consistency of the reports, especially among soldiers who had not shared stories with one another, challenged this explanation.
Psychological Evaluation of Troops: Military psychologists who assessed the troops found that while many were under severe stress, the specific and recurring nature of the sightings did not fit typical patterns of hallucination. Many soldiers insisted that what they saw felt real, not like an illusion or a figment of their imagination.
Equipment Replacement (1971): By 1971, the red-tinted night vision goggles were replaced with green-tinted versions that offered clearer visibility without the reddish hue. After this switch, reports of supernatural entities ceased almost entirely, suggesting a possible link between the red light spectrum and the phenomena.
Documented Phenomena
Eyewitness Testimonies: Numerous testimonies from soldiers describe encounters with shadowy entities and winged demons. These witnesses reported experiences that left them traumatized, often struggling to describe what they saw without sounding “crazy.”

Unexplained Equipment Malfunctions: Several soldiers noted that their radios or other electronic equipment would malfunction during sightings, adding to the strangeness of the encounters. These malfunctions were never fully explained, though they were often attributed to interference from the thick jungle.

Psychological Impact: Many soldiers reported long-lasting fear and paranoia after their encounters, some experiencing recurring nightmares or feeling as though they were being watched.
Press Coverage and Public Reaction
The US military never publicly acknowledged these sightings during or after the war, and reports of these encounters remained confined to military circles and veteran communities. However, stories of the red night vision goggles and the terrifying encounters soon spread among those with a taste for the paranormal, becoming the subject of speculation and conspiracy theories. Some believe the US military was aware of a supernatural presence in Vietnam and intentionally withheld information, while others dismiss the accounts as stress-induced hallucinations.
Case Status

This case was closed following the replacement of the red night vision goggles with green-tinted models. Despite the lack of a formal investigation or conclusive explanation, many Vietnam veterans continue to share stories of their encounters, believing they witnessed something that defied understanding.
File Archived: Case Closed – Equipment Replaced, Explanation Inconclusive
Location: MILITARY ARCHIVES – Classified
The Story
The Phantom Patrol

In 1968, deep within the jungles of Vietnam, a reconnaissance team was assigned a routine patrol along a treacherous river trail known for enemy ambushes. As the night wore on, the soldiers donned their red-tinted infrared night vision goggles to scan the dense foliage surrounding them. Hours into their patrol, one of the soldiers froze, his eyes locked on a figure in the distance. It looked humanoid but impossibly thin, its limbs too long, and its movements unnaturally fluid.

The soldier whispered a warning to the rest of the team, each turning to see the figure now standing among the trees, staring back at them with piercing, red-glowing eyes. As the team attempted to maneuver around the entity, more figures appeared in the shadows, each one twisting and contorting as though bound to some dark force within the jungle. A low murmur filled the air, growing into a chorus of overlapping whispers that seemed to seep into their minds, urging them forward.

Overcome with a sudden, inexplicable dread, the team’s leader ordered them to retreat. The soldiers turned and bolted, feeling the heavy gaze of those unnatural figures on their backs as they ran. After regrouping, they shared uneasy glances but dared not speak of what they had seen. They returned to base in silence, haunted by the memory of those entities lurking in the jungle, watching, waiting.

The Winged Demons of the Night
One of the most disturbing accounts came from a helicopter gunner in 1970 during a night mission. As his unit flew over a dense, moonlit stretch of jungle, he scanned the ground below with his machine gun ready. The night was quiet, with only the rhythmic hum of the helicopter breaking the silence. Suddenly, he saw movement in the air around him—a huge, dark shape swooping through the sky, its wings flapping in slow, powerful beats.

The gunner blinked, thinking he was seeing things, but then another creature appeared on the opposite side, keeping pace with the helicopter. He opened fire, emptying round after round into the night, trying to hit the figure as it glided beside him. In the chaos, his fellow gunner shouted, “What the hell are you shooting at?” but he could barely respond, paralyzed by the sight of the creature’s massive, leathery wings and glowing red eyes.

One by one, other shapes appeared, circling the helicopter like predators stalking prey. The gunners opened fire wildly, desperately trying to fend off the creatures that seemed impervious to bullets. The creatures moved with impossible grace, their hollow eyes staring through the gunner as though studying him. In that moment, he felt an overwhelming sense of dread, as if these beings were ancient and malevolent, drawn to the noise and chaos of war.

When the helicopter finally landed, the gunner could barely stand, his hands trembling. He tried to explain what he had seen, but his fellow soldiers dismissed it as a hallucination brought on by stress. Despite this, the gunner knew he had seen something beyond human understanding, and the memory of those winged demons haunted him long after the war.

The Haunting of Firebase Ripcord

In 1971, a platoon stationed at Firebase Ripcord reported frequent sightings of shadowy figures in the jungle around their perimeter. The base was often targeted by enemy forces, but these figures were different—larger than a human, with grotesque, elongated limbs and eyes that glowed when seen through the red night vision goggles.

One night, as the men scanned the jungle with their goggles, they saw several of these beings circling the base, moving in patterns that seemed almost deliberate. Suddenly, a gunner on watch began firing into the treeline, shouting that one of the creatures was charging the base. Other soldiers joined in, firing round after round, but the figures simply faded into the darkness, leaving an unsettling silence.

The attacks and sightings continued for weeks, intensifying morale issues and sparking fear among the soldiers. The men felt as though something was watching them, waiting for a moment to strike. Finally, following a series of encounters that left several soldiers in a state of shock, the unit received green-tinted night vision goggles, ending the terrifying sightings. To this day, survivors of Firebase Ripcord speak of the dark entities that prowled around their base, hidden from the light, haunting their memories.

These cases, despite their lack of official acknowledgment, suggest that Vietnam was not only a battlefield of human conflict but perhaps a realm where supernatural forces emerged, drawn to the chaos, feeding on fear. The entities remain a mystery, confined to the red hue of those early night vision goggles, and forever etched into the minds of the soldiers who faced them.

text:
Kevin Garnett says he opened USA Today in Jamaica and saw a headline that he had denied $122 million. He says he never got to deny it. His agent did.

In the video below, Kevin Garnett says, "I probably would have took the 122."

It was August 1997. Garnett was 21, in the last year of his rookie contract, making about $2.1 million. The Minnesota Timberwolves had offered a six-year deal worth about $103.2 million. Owner Glen Taylor said he was disappointed that agent Eric Fleisher had turned the offer down.

Garnett says he had a bowl of fruit in his lap when he read it, spilled it, and flew home. He says he told the agent not to speak for him, and that he fired him.

On October 1, 1997, Garnett signed a six-year contract reported at $126 million, then the largest in team sports. Fleisher was still named as his agent on that deal. The Associated Press later put the salary total at $128.1 million, all guaranteed, rising from $14 million the next season to $28 million in the last year.

He stayed in Minnesota, won the 2004 MVP, and in 2008 won a title with Boston.

So did Garnett's agent cost him a voice in that $122 million, or did turning it down get him the biggest contract in sports?

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

July 4, 1187. After the Crusader army was destroyed at the Horns of Hattin, Saladin singled out the captured members of the two military orders—the Knights Templar and Hospitallers (roughly 200 men). Imad ad-Din al-Isfahani, Saladin’s secretary and an eyewitness, records that the sultan declared he would “purify the land of these two impure races,” paid fifty dinars a head to buy them from their captors so none could be ransomed or spared, and ordered them beheaded. Scholars, Sufis, and other religious men carried out the executions while Saladin watched with evident satisfaction. Contemporary Muslim and Christian accounts record the same mass beheading and the offer of conversion to Islam, which the knights refused to a man. 

828 years later, on 15 February 2015, ISIS released a video titled “A Message Signed with Blood to the Nation of the Cross.” It showed 21 Egyptian Coptic Christian migrant workers dressed in orange jumpsuits—unarmed laborers from poor villages in Upper Egypt—forced to kneel on a beach and brutally beheaded. Some called out “Lord Jesus Christ” as they died. The accompanying text and narration framed them as “people of the cross” and followers of the “hostile Egyptian Church”—a community present in Egypt for six hundred years before Islam even existed.

In both cases, Muslim forces beheaded non-Muslim captives who rejected conversion to Islam. The method (forced kneeling followed by decapitation) and the explicit religious justification were the same. Saladin is one of Islam’s greatest and most celebrated heroes; the men who carried out the 2015 killings were not operating outside the Islamic tradition he embodied. These men were not “Islamic radicals” or some aberrant Muslim sect that failed to understand the true Islam. If anything, they more accurately represent the historic, Qur’an-observant, traditional form—not the nominal or Westernized version, but the modern expression of a fourteen-century pattern that has not changed:

text:
When History Stops Being a Warning

by Elisabeth Sabaditsch-Wolff

The blue wave that swept across America this week has left me deeply uncomfortable. Not because the Democrats won. That’s democracy. People go to the polls, cast their votes, and sometimes the result is one we don’t particularly like. I can live with that, even when I profoundly disagree with the political direction the voters have chosen.

What I find much harder to live with is the enthusiasm surrounding the victories, the almost gleeful celebration of political developments that remind me of things I have seen before. At least five members of the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization with a caucus that openly calls itself Marxist-Leninist, are on their way to Congress, and when she won her primary in June, one of them, Claire Valdez of New York, said: “We have declared that this movement is durable.” I believe her. And I cannot help wondering whether those celebrating have any idea why people like me find this so troubling.

I spent four formative years in America during the Reagan era, when communism was not some distant historical curiosity. We learned about it in school. We watched the news from Moscow and Eastern Europe. We knew about the Berlin Wall, about people risking their lives to escape communist countries, and about the fundamental difference between a society in which the individual was free and one in which the state determined the limits of that freedom.

In November 1988, I stood in East Berlin. I had crossed from West Berlin into a world that could hardly have been more different, and what I saw confirmed everything I had learned. I still vividly remember bustling West Berlin, the Kurfürstendamm with its sparkling lights in the dark November nights, and then, on the other side of Checkpoint Charlie, the drabness, the grayness and the palpable despair of a destroyed society. I decided then and there that I did not want to live in a society governed by socialism. Not now, not ever. I have never forgotten that experience.

Nor have I forgotten Iran.

I was there during the Iranian Revolution of 1979, as a child of seven. I watched a country undergo an ideological transformation, and only years later did I learn how it had come about, with leftists and Khomeini’s followers united in their opposition to the Shah. Their common enemy brought them together, but it did not mean they shared the same vision for Iran’s future. By 1983 the Communist Tudeh party was banned and its leaders were in prison, and in 1988 — the same year I stood in East Berlin — thousands of political prisoners were executed, leftists among them.

These experiences shaped my political convictions long before I had ever heard of Friedrich A. Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, or Murray Rothbard. When I eventually encountered their writings, I found an understanding of individual liberty that made perfect sense to me. Hayek, in particular, understood liberty as freedom from arbitrary coercion, with government constrained by the rule of law rather than empowered to direct people’s lives according to some grand political vision. Having witnessed what happens when those constraints disappear and the individual becomes subordinate to an ideology, his arguments resonated with me immediately.

That is why I find the current enthusiasm so difficult to understand.

America has been home to generations of people who fled communism, religious persecution, and authoritarian governments. They came because America represented something different. It offered the possibility of living without the state or a religious authority dictating every aspect of their lives. And yet I now watch Americans celebrating political ideas and alliances without asking the questions whose answers history has already taught us.

I am not suggesting that every Democrat is a communist, or that every Democratic victory is a step toward totalitarianism. That would be far too simplistic. What concerns me is the growing acceptance of socialist ideas, the attraction of communism among some on the left, and the willingness to overlook fundamental ideological differences in pursuit of political power.

Perhaps what troubles me most is the apparent absence of historical memory. We seem increasingly willing to judge political movements by what they promise rather than by what comparable movements have done when given power.

And that brings me to the question I cannot shake.

What happens when people no longer recognize the warning signs? What happens when they celebrate political developments without considering where those developments might lead? And what happens when they finally recognize the danger, only to discover that reversing course has become extraordinarily difficult?

I am not angry that Americans voted differently from how I would have liked. What I feel is apprehension about what lies ahead, rooted in experiences I cannot simply set aside.

Having seen East Berlin and lived through the Iranian Revolution, I know how profoundly political systems can change and how easily freedoms once taken for granted can disappear.

For much of my life, America represented the place to which people could flee when freedom disappeared elsewhere.

But what happens if America itself ceases to be that place?

Where will people go then?

ROUND XVI
AS THEY ARE
A CITIZEN'S DAMNATION OF THE MIDDLEMEN IN THE GULF, AND A CONDEMNATION OF THE ROYAL HOUSES THAT LET THEM IN

Raised by a citizen of the United States under the Constitution and the Declaration of Independence, and laid before the President and the Congress in exercise of the right "to petition the Government for a redress of grievances"

AGAINST the middlemen in the Gulf: the British and French states, damned in Rounds VII and III; the European Union's Commission and agencies, charged in Rounds I and IX; the banks and bureaus that answer to no nation; and the networks that rent the region's free zones.

AND, in condemnation, the seven ruling houses of the Gulf and the five emirates beside them, for the doors they opened and for their record against Americans.

Not against the peoples of the Gulf. Not against the sovereignty of any house. Sovereignty is the point.

I. THE RULE

Our own strategy, November 2025: "The world's fundamental political unit is and will remain the nation-state." It stands "against the sovereignty-sapping incursions of the most intrusive transnational organizations." Of the Gulf, it ends "America's misguided experiment with hectoring these nations—especially the Gulf monarchies—into abandoning their traditions and historic forms of government," and accepts "the region, its leaders, and its nations as they are."

As they are: absolute monarchies on the trade routes of the world. An absolute monarchy is worth one thing to a sovereign republic: a sovereign it can deal with directly, state to state. Without absolute control, it is of no use to anyone. The rule holds for every capital: two signatures where it can be done, and never a signature that is not a state's.

II. YOUR OWN SIGNATURE

Your rulers signed your founding laws. You will be judged by them.

Saudi Arabia, Basic Law, Art. 44: "The King shall be the point of reference for all these authorities."
Kuwait, Art. 1: "There shall be no surrender of its sovereignty."
Bahrain, Art. 1: "Its sovereignty shall not be ceded."
Qatar, Art. 1: "Qatar is an independent sovereign Arab State."
The UAE, Art. 4: "The UAE may not cede its sovereignty."
Oman, Basic Statute, Art. 1: an "independent state with full sovereignty."

In 1776 we charged a king with combining "with others to subject us to a jurisdiction foreign to our constitution, and unacknowledged by our laws." You did it to your own.

III. WHAT WE SIGNED

21 September 1833, Muscat: Edmund Roberts and Said bin Sultan. "There shall be a perpetual peace." Two signatures, fifty-nine years before London's Exclusive Agreements; replaced at Salalah in 1958, again by two. 14 February 1945, the USS Quincy: Roosevelt and Ibn Saud. Two men. No third.

Investment paper with all six, 1975 to 1992: the footing of our Development Finance Corporation. Free trade agreements with Bahrain and Oman; trade frameworks with four.

22 October 2025: Doha and Washington wrote together to Europe's heads of state, around the Commission. 17 November 2025: Riyadh and Washington settled motor-vehicle standards between themselves, after Riyadh had drifted toward Geneva's. That is the template.

We kept faith. This is what was done with the space between us.

IV. THE MIDDLEMEN

LONDON. The first middleman, and by force. 1819: your navy shelled Ras Al Khaimah. Then the treaties of 1820, 1853 and 1892, the last binding the rulers to deal with no power but you. You held their foreign relations until 1971, and replaced rulers who displeased you: Abu Dhabi, 1966; Muscat, 1970. In 1968 you left the Gulf over our objection and banked what we stayed to guard (Round VII). Al-Yamamah: your fraud office dropped it in 2006 after your Prime Minister intervened; BAE pleaded guilty in our court in 2010 and paid $400 million. 2008: Qatari money saved Barclays for the City; your fraud office called £322 million in side fees a fraud, charged the bank and five of its men, and convicted no one.

PARIS. 26 May 2009, Abu Dhabi: opening your base, you pledged to help defend a house's security, sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence, and signed a pact on its internal security. The Louvre's name, leased to a house since 2007. A 2008 tax amendment sparing Qatar's state capital-gains tax on French property. Gulf money landing in fourteen African states as CFA francs rests on your Treasury's guarantee. Your state lender sits beside the EBRD in a house's flagship plants in Uzbekistan.

BRUSSELS. 28 September 2026: Eurojust signed a working arrangement with Abu Dhabi's ministry of justice. Eighteen days earlier your Commission asked to open talks on full agreements with the UAE and seven states of our hemisphere, Canada among them: a house's courts and our hemisphere, in one document. Your Council agreed on 29 October. Your gatekeepers listed the UAE for money laundering in 2023 and delisted it in 2025. Qatargate: members of your Parliament charged over money alleged to come from Doha, which Doha denies.

THE BANKS AND BUREAUS. Riyadh's, Abu Dhabi's and Kuwait's central banks hold shares in Basel (Round IV), whose hub built mBridge with Beijing and the UAE's central bank. Davos (Round X) met in Riyadh in 2024. The Fund: in October, $18.3 billion of Riyadh's, Kuwait's and Doha's deposits sat at Egypt's central bank, assured to the IMF until its programme ends on 15 December 2026, except as equity, and filed in the Fund's own multilateral column. A house's word to a sovereign, rewritten as a bureau's.

THE NETWORKS. No house, sovereign fund or Gulf state body is on Washington's, London's or Brussels' sanctions lists. Their free zones are: 768 entries on our Treasury's list carry an Emirati address, Iran's networks first; 203 on London's, most Russia's; 41 on Brussels'. The RSF kept a financial adviser and proxy companies in Dubai (UN Panel of Experts, 2024). In 2019 the UAE recorded 80,986 kilograms of gold from Mali; Mali declared 567 (UNODC). Islamic Relief: funded by Brussels and London, seated at the UN. London reviewed the Brotherhood in 2015 and declined to ban it.

IRAN. The artery through all of it. This year it fired on every one of you, and on our people in your bases. On 11 March the Security Council condemned it, 13 to none, in Resolution 2817, tabled by Bahrain. Moscow and Beijing abstained.

V. THE HOUSES, AND THEIR RECORD

From our own records and the United Nations'. Your nationals are not your state: a count stands only on the state's own conduct, with what cuts against it beside it.

You have replaced weak hands yourselves: Riyadh, 1964; Doha, 1972 and 1995. You know what a ruler is for.

AL SAUD. Your throne does not run to the Prophet. It runs to the USS Quincy. In August, at Mecca, you signed with Islamabad and Ankara to carry your own defence, as our strategy asks, and our President welcomed it; then you wrote a NATO member into it and barred the exit for ten years. If your war reaches Turkish soil, it reaches Article 5.
1. 1967, 1973. Oil held back from us, then "a total embargo on oil exports to the United States."
2. 1972–80. American-owned Aramco, taken by stages; the first quarter paid at about twice book value.
3. 1988. Chinese CSS-2 missiles, bought "unknown to us." Our ambassador, objecting, was left "no alternative" but to leave.
4. 2000–01. Fifteen of the nineteen hijackers were your nationals. The 9/11 Commission: "no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded" al Qaeda; our Joint Inquiry: some hijackers "received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government."
5. 2001–08. You "failed to impose criminal punishment on any high-profile donor." Our Treasury, 2008: "Saudi Arabia today remains the location from which more money is going to terror groups and the Taliban."
6. 2008. Your official textbooks, taught in Virginia by "an arm of the Saudi government," still carried "overt exhortations to violence" (USCIRF).
7. 2015–25. Cited for not returning abducted American children. Ten are still not home.
8. 2014–15. A royal's office paid a Twitter insider for data on critics. Convicted in 2022 as your agent; one count later reversed on venue.
9. 2016–20. Your consulate paid $100,000 to free the student who killed Fallon Smart, the prosecutor said; he fled. The FBI: "Saudi Officials Almost Certainly Assist Saudi Citizens Flee the United States."
10. 2017–21. Walid Fitaihi, an American doctor, held without charge; his family, "all of whom are U.S. citizens," barred from leaving.
11. 2018. Jamal Khashoggi, a US resident and Post columnist, killed in your Istanbul consulate. Our intelligence: the Crown Prince "approved an operation in Istanbul, Turkey to capture or kill" him. You reject it.
12. 2022. Saad Almadi, seventy-two, of Florida: sixteen years for fourteen tweets.
13. 2022. An OPEC+ cut with Moscow, over our objection that "there was no market basis." You called that "not based on facts."

AL NAHYAN. A founder of mBridge. A member of BRICS. Since 6 October 2026, party to a trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union: five states, with a commission over them. Your services and investment pact with Moscow, 7 August 2025, carried two signatures. The rule is the same for Moscow as for Brussels: the state, never its commission. You banned the Brotherhood and listed Islamic Relief in 2014, then invited in the prosecutors of Brussels, which has funded it.
1. 1973. Abu Dhabi "announced or threatened a total embargo" on us.
2. 1990–2010. "Nuclear traffickers shipped via the UAE because the UAE lacked significant export control laws" (House, 2010).
3. 1997–2001. You recognised the Taliban and stayed one of its "only travel and financial outlets."
4. 1999. Bin Ladin, at a hunting camp beside "an official aircraft of the United Arab Emirates." No strike, for fear of killing a prince. A week after we raised it with Muhammad bin Zayid, the camp was "hurriedly dismantled." He denied officials were there.
5. 2000–01. Nine hijackers transited Dubai; the money moved through UAE accounts; one hijacker "received a salary from the UAE military." The Commission found no evidence of foreign-government funding.
6. 2012. The US-funded National Democratic Institute shut; its American director briefly barred from leaving.
7. 2013. Shezanne Cassim, an American, jailed nine months over a parody video.
8. 2016–19. Raven: former US intelligence operatives hacked for you, into US computers (Justice Department); deferred prosecution, 2021.
9. 2015–19. US weapons passed to Yemeni militias (CNN). Our CENTCOM commander: "We have not authorized Saudi Arabia or the Emirates to retransfer any of this equipment." You deny it.
10. 2019–20. A Pantsir to Haftar under a UN arms embargo (UN panel); you "may provide some financing" for Wagner (DIA). You deny it.
11. 2021. A Chinese facility at Khalifa Port, halted under our pressure: "we stopped the work."
12. 2022–23. Treasury's "country of focus" for Russia-sanctions evasion.
13. 2023–26. Flights from Abu Dhabi to the RSF: "credible" to the UN panel in 2024, unconfirmed in 2025. Treasury sanctioned seven RSF companies in the UAE. You deny arming either side.

AL MAKTOUM. Your free zones are the address book of other men's sanctions, and the gold scale of the Sahel. The fronts register with you. The proxies bank with you. The gold weighs in with you.
1. 1990s–2003. A Dubai firm was "a front for the proliferation activities of the A.Q. Khan network" (President Bush); no US document finds your officials complicit.
2. 2011. Noor Bank, part-owned by your government and chaired by the ruler's son, carried up to 60 percent of Iran's foreign oil sales, US officials estimated.

AL THANI. The open door. Al-Qaradawi preached from Doha for sixty years.
1. 1992–96. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed worked in your Ministry of Electricity and Water. Indicted by us, he escaped: "an official in the government of Qatar probably warned him about it."
2. 2008–15. Al Qaeda financiers designated while living in Qatar. Our Treasury, 2014: "such a permissive terrorist financing environment," a state that had "for many years openly financed Hamas."
3. 2012–24. Hamas's office in Doha. You say Washington asked. A channel was asked for. A home was given. In 2024 we told you its leaders were no longer welcome.
4. 2014. The Huangs, Americans acquitted by your court, held at your airport by a travel ban; our Secretary of State had to call.
5. 2017. For royal hunters held in Iraq, your envoy flew in "hundreds of millions of dollars," seized by Iraq's prime minister as bound for armed groups. You say it went to the Iraqi state.
6. 2020–24. Your state network's American arm, told to register as a foreign agent, had not by 2024.

AL SABAH. Your fund was born in London in 1953, signed with Britain's political agent eight years before your independence: that birth is London's charge. That its office is there still is yours. Since 2025 you levy the minimum tax Paris's tax club wrote.
1. 1967, 1973. You resolved "to stop all oil exports to the United States." The 1973 embargo, decided in Kuwait, reached "refiners supplying U.S. forces in Bahrain, Italy and Greece."
2. 1975–77. Gulf Oil's half of the Kuwait Oil Company, taken by agreement. Aminoil's concession, ended by decree; a tribunal found it lawful, with about $179 million in compensation.
3. 1987. You asked Moscow, too, to escort your tankers. We came.
4. 2008. Your minister called our designation of the Revival of Islamic Heritage Society "unfounded."
5. 2014. "Our ally Kuwait has become the epicenter of fundraising for terrorist groups in Syria" (Treasury). Your new justice minister had "a history of promoting jihad in Syria." He resigned.
6. 2015–16. Your state airline refused an Israeli passenger out of New York, and dropped the route rather than obey our Transportation Department.
7. 2025. On our Treasury's list of states requiring "participation in, or cooperation with, an international boycott."

AL KHALIFA. London's officials put a British officer into your security service in 1966: that is London's charge. You kept him at its head until 1998, twenty-six years after your independence: that is yours.
1. 1973, 1975. An embargo and notice ending our Navy's station, then an order that it leave "by June 30, 1977." The Fleet stayed.
2. 2006. The US National Democratic Institute's director's visa revoked.
3. 2012. American protest observers arrested and deported.
4. 2014. Our Assistant Secretary of State ordered out for meeting the opposition alone. Our Secretary of State called your demand "unacceptable."
5. 2014. A member of our Congress refused a guarantee of entry.
6. 2016. Four American journalists arrested and charged.

AL SAID. Duqm opened to a Chinese industrial park. Thirty-two entries on our Treasury's list carry an Omani address.
1. 1980. With Americans hostage in Tehran: "Oman to give Iraq access to facilities for attack on Iran" (our embassy). Qaboos dropped it.
2. 2016–20. Iran's arms for the Houthis crossed your land and waters; the UN found no evidence of your complicity.
3. 2025–26. The Houthis' "Oman-based spokesman," designated by our Treasury, is in Muscat still. Our embassy has met him there.
4. 2025–26. Bank Muscat, majority state-owned, refuses US remittance services on "unwritten guidance from the Central Bank" (USTR).
5. 2026. In the war, no facilities and no bases for us, your foreign minister said.
6. 2026. Our President: "Nobody is going to control it." Our Treasury Secretary: "Oman, in particular." On 25 August you and Tehran announced "a joint temporary navigational corridor through the Strait of Hormuz."

THE FIVE EMIRATES. 18 December 2025: our Treasury named a ship manager in Sharjah's Hamriyah Free Zone, and four of its tankers, in Iran's shadow fleet. Ras Al Khaimah was shelled into the first middleman's arms in 1819: London's charge.

IN OUR CAPITAL. The middlemen run both ways. From 2001 to 2021 foreign agents filed 148 registrations for principals in Saudi Arabia, 130 for the UAE, 108 for Qatar (Congressional Research Service). In 2025 our universities reported over $1.1 billion from Qatar, more than from any other country. A house that wants two signatures does not rent a third.

Washington has stopped asking you to change. It is asking you to rule.

VI. WHAT WE GAVE

The Quincy, 1945. Escorts for your tankers, 1987 and 1988. Over half a million Americans to free Kuwait and guard Arabia, 1990 and 1991. The Fifth Fleet in Manama. Al Udeid, Al Dhafra, Arifjan. This year our bases on your soil took Iran's fire. On 14 July our President dropped the 20 percent Hormuz fee set the day before and asked the Gulf states for trade and investment deals into the United States instead.

Washington and Moscow drained their treasuries here. We paid in blood. You paid in legitimacy, as sovereign absolute monarchies. What comes next is for the nations involved to settle, not for bureaus and banks in Europe that answer to no nation.

VII. DAMNATION

A navy that shelled its way in and held the rulers' foreign relations until 1971. A fraud case dropped when a Prime Minister intervened. Paris written into a house's defence. A guarantee from Paris under the money of fourteen African states. Prosecutors signed in by working arrangement. Rails laid with Beijing. A house's word to Cairo, filed as a bureau's. Free zones that keep the address book of other men's sanctions. And the houses that opened the doors, with fifty-three counts against Americans on record.

From 1819 to 2026, by their own records, the United Nations' and ours, the middlemen in the Gulf stand damned. The houses that let them in stand condemned under their own founding laws.

There is no reprieve.

THE TERMS I WOULD SET

I hold no office and set no terms. Terms with a foreign power are the President's to set and the Department of State's to carry, and to both I defer. The purse is the Congress's. What touches national security is deferred, without contest. These would be the terms.

I. Off Beijing's rails: Abu Dhabi's central bank out of mBridge. Our strategy rewards those who "align their export controls with ours."
II. Close the arteries: the fronts in your free zones, the ship-to-ship trade in Iran's oil, the registries. Iran's oil and money stop at your ports.
III. Sudan: the RSF's money out of your free zones.
IV. The Brotherhood and Hamas, judged by conduct. A list binds no one. A door does.
V. States, not commissions, in Eurasia as in Brussels: the EAEU agreement replaced by two-signature pacts, state by state.
VI. Cairo: when the Fund's programme ends on 15 December, every Gulf deposit, renewed or converted, goes house to state, out of the multilateral column.
VII. Brussels: no full Eurojust agreement; no European benchmark riding on Gulf money.
VIII. Our own compacts: two signatures from here on. We invited London into Bahrain's compact; that door is ours to close from 20 October 2028.
IX. Standards: ours, set two at a time, as Riyadh did in November 2025.
X. Tether or door. The charters states made, we hold to their text. The banks and bureaus that seat non-state members, or that we never signed, get the door: the EBRD, Basel, Davos. The houses' seats in Basel go with ours. The houses' own institutions are the houses' business.
XI. Our people: Americans held or barred from leaving, freed; abducted children, home; fugitives from our courts, returned.
XII. No shelter: designated financiers prosecuted or surrendered; no home for Hamas or the Houthis' sanctioned spokesman; no Hormuz toll or corridor without us.

To London, Paris and Brussels, and the banks and bureaus beside them: you have been told.
Your exits are already filed: Rounds I, II, III, IV and VII.

THE DOOR
Guidance, respectfully offered to the offices that hold the power this author does not.

No new treaty is needed. Our direct institutions exist: "the International Development Finance Corporation; the Export-Import Bank; and the Millennium Challenge Corporation." The President named the door on 14 July 2026. Two signatures. No third.

THE HINGES
A door that cannot close is not a door. Two signatures opened each of these; either one can close it. The hinges are how the terms are kept. From our own Treaties in Force: 129 entries under the six, 72 read against their texts. Not a recommendation: what the Executive CAN do alone.
ON NOTICE. Air transport, Abu Dhabi (TIAS 02-1211), Doha (20-827), Kuwait (07-527), Muscat (15-116), Manama (13035): a year, the notice sent "simultaneously to the International Civil Aviation Organization" (Art. 15). Even the exit is copied to a bureau. Preclearance, Abu Dhabi (13-1208): twelve months, or one, by us alone, if the UAE falls short of its Art. III. Investment guaranties, Riyadh (8045) and Muscat (8651): six months; cover written survives up to twenty years. Trade frameworks, Riyadh (03-731), Muscat (04-707), Kuwait, Abu Dhabi: six months. Riyadh's National Guard program (7634): six months. Our training mission in Riyadh (8558), and Kuwait's defense procurement and our liaison office (8066): a year. Riyadh's civil technical cooperation (23-508): ninety days.
THE COMPACT WE OPENED. Bahrain (23-1020), London a party since 19 June 2025: no withdrawal before 20 October 2028, then six months (Art. IX). Its implementing arrangements outlive it.
CONGRESS SIGNED THESE. Free trade with Bahrain (Art. 21.5; Pub. L. 109-169) and Oman (Art. 22.5; Pub. L. 109-283): 180 days. Whether a President may withdraw alone is contested ground.
THE SENATE'S SHELF. The Bahrain investment treaty (13065, Art. 16): a year, existing investments protected ten more. The Salalah treaty with Oman (4530, Art. XVI): a year.
KEPT, AND KEPT FOR A REASON. They protect Americans: ICC non-surrender, consular immunities, customs, crime and visa cooperation, Leahy vetting, FATCA, our carriers' tax exemptions, work for our diplomats' families, passage for our Afghan partners, the Peace Corps, our jurisdiction over Riyadh's ships at the Louisiana Offshore Oil Port.
THE DEAD PAPER. Under Kuwait, a 1951 consular convention signed by Washington and London, ratified at London: Kuwait never signed it, and its exit runs between London and us, six months (Art. 29). Under Saudi Arabia, our first agreement with the house, signed in London in 1933, "until the entry in force of a definitive treaty of commerce and navigation." The book lists none. Thirty days, or at once if Congress stops us carrying it out. Under Oman, a science agreement signed at Davos, its term run out on 31 March 2026 unless renewed. Stale or spent: a 1958 Dammam port grant, two F-86 agreements, a paragraph of 1953, and UN Compensation Commission guidelines whose last payment the UN dates to 2022.
THE MULTILATERALS. Three name a house: two wartime declarations, and the Middle East Desalination Research Center, Muscat, 1996, with Israel, Japan, Korea and Oman, open to intergovernmental members: six months (Art. 10(b)).
NOT IN THE BOOK. Four defence cooperation agreements and Riyadh's of November 2025; the 2012 framework with the Gulf Cooperation Council, a bloc, not in force per UNCTAD.
THE PAPER WE CANNOT READ. Ten deferred without contest. Three nuclear: recorded, never offered. Eighteen unpublished. Twenty-six out of open reach.

OUR OWN LEDGER

Two signatures means no invited third and no private third. We built our 2023 security compact with Bahrain open to new members; we and Manama invited London in December 2024. Our own money rides in the middle: Gulf capital in American funds, American giants in the houses' AI ventures, ventures close to our own government. We are the EBRD's largest shareholder, lead the World Bank, whose Rogun group holds four houses' funds, and sit in the Fund that files their deposits as multilateral. Washington: close those doors too.

TO THOSE WHO DO HOLD THE POWER

I make no demand of you. I set beside each office the power it already holds.
The President: the footing, the agreements and the template.
The Congress: the purse, and oversight of every dollar here.
The Treasury: the lists, and the free zones on them.
The Secretary of State: two signatures, house by house, and the air agreements.
The Secretary of Defense: the National Guard program.
The Trade Representative: the free trade agreements and trade frameworks.
The Attorney General: the foreign-agent files.
The Secretary of Education: Section 117.
The Development Finance Corporation: what you back under the investment agreements.

The sixteenth. Read it with all that came before.

We the People

Copying @BIS_org @EBRD @IMFNews @wef @UN @EU_Commission @Eurojust @OECD , so nobody feels left out.

ROUND XVII is loaded.

AFL reclaims grand final TV crown from NRL

(Original article by Sam Buckingham-Jones)
(RMS)

Data from OzTAM shows that the Nine Network's coverage of the NRL grand final on Sunday night boasted an average audience of 4.29 million people. Some 1.45 million people also watched the premiership decider via the 9Now app, and the match had a total audience reach of 6.05 million. In contrast, the previous weekend's AFL grand final attracted an average audience of 4.52 million on the Seven Network, and a total audience reach of 6.5 million. Ben Willee from Spinach Advertising says the fact that both codes attracted more than six million viewers underlines the value of live sport for both advertiser and broadcasters. (RMS)

Miners stay top of ATO's taxpayer table
(RMS)

The Australian Taxation Office's latest corporate tax transparency report shows that the nation's largest companies paid $87.5bn in taxes during 2024-25. Rio Tinto topped the list with $5.2bn in taxes, ahead of BHP with a total company tax bill of $3.9bn. The Mining, Energy and Water sector contributed 41.1 per cent of the corporate tax take, or $35.9bn; this was $12.5bn lower than previously, due to weaker commodity prices. The data also shows that the petroleum resource rent tax raised $1.9bn in 2024-25. (RMS)

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. (RMS)

News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

EVENING DISPATCH UPDATE
Tuesday, November 10, 2026

Reports from across the Denver metro area this afternoon and evening included an armed carjacking followed by a regional vehicle search, an assault on a law enforcement officer leading to a high-speed pursuit, several weapons complaints, a possible explosion in Lakewood, multiple serious traffic collisions, and several incidents involving public transportation.

Other notable calls included an injured puppy reportedly abandoned at an Aurora restaurant, reports of aggressive dogs and wildlife concerns, and a possible hit-and-run near Lookout Mountain.

The following information is based on publicly available emergency dispatch communications. Details are preliminary, and investigations or responses may still be ongoing.

JEFFERSON COUNTY / LAKEWOOD / ARVADA / GOLDEN

5:24 PM | LAKEWOOD | VEHICLE COLLISION

Emergency crews were dispatched to a reported motor vehicle collision near West Hopi Avenue and Sheridan Boulevard. Engine 1 and Medic 11 were assigned to the response.

5:22 PM | LAKEWOOD | MEDICAL RESPONSE

Dispatch traffic referenced a medical response near Kipling Street, with additional radio communications mentioning Highway 285 and Highway 121. The exact circumstances were not established.

5:22 PM | C-470 | DISABLED VEHICLE

A disabled vehicle was reported on eastbound C-470 near Kipling Parkway. The vehicle was reportedly on the right shoulder.

5:08 PM | ARVADA | TWO PATIENTS REPORTED

Fire crews were dispatched to a residence in the West 71st Avenue area after a caller reported two people requiring assistance. The nature and severity of the medical situation were not immediately available.

5:06 PM | KIPLING AND PROGRESS | VEHICLE COLLISION

A Subaru and a Jeep were reportedly involved in a crash near South Kipling Parkway and West Progress Avenue. Both vehicles were said to be obstructing the intersection, and medical responders were requested.

5:05 PM | NORTH TURKEY CREEK AREA | INJURY CRASH

Jefferson County fire dispatch reported a possible motor vehicle injury crash near Westway Drive. The call referenced southbound Highway 25, although the mapped location and roadway information were inconsistent. The exact crash location requires confirmation.

5:00 PM | LAKEWOOD | WADSWORTH AND MISSISSIPPI

Police requested medical assistance following a reported injury crash near South Wadsworth Boulevard and West Mississippi Avenue. The medical response was described as nonemergent.

4:55 PM | GOLDEN | POSSIBLE HIT-AND-RUN

Dispatch communications referenced a possible hit-and-run involving a white vehicle near Lookout Mountain Road. Separate radio traffic mentioned a possible collision involving a BMW and a bicyclist. It remains unclear whether the reports concern the same incident.

4:51 PM | LITTLETON AREA | ELEVATOR RESCUE

Emergency crews acknowledged a report of people possibly trapped inside a hotel elevator on South Elkhorn Street. The automated location information also referenced South Alkire Street, so the precise location remains unconfirmed.

4:19 PM | C-470 AND WADSWORTH | TRAFFIC COMPLAINT

A motorist reported another vehicle allegedly throwing objects toward their vehicle while traveling eastbound on C-470 near Wadsworth Boulevard. Additional law enforcement assistance was requested.

4:06 PM | LAKEWOOD | POSSIBLE OVERDOSE

Emergency crews were dispatched to an apartment on West Second Place near White Street for a reported overdose or poisoning involving a person who was unconscious or nearly fainting.

3:19 PM | LAKEWOOD | MULTIPLE PATIENTS REPORTED IN CRASH

Emergency crews were dispatched to a collision near West Alameda Parkway and South Youngfield Court. Initial radio traffic referenced five patients. Their injuries and conditions were not confirmed in the available summary.

3:19 PM | LAKEWOOD | CEDAR AND GARRISON CRASH

Fire and medical units were dispatched for a reported collision near West Cedar Avenue and South Garrison Street. Subsequent radio traffic indicated responding units were told to disregard the call.

3:14 PM | WADSWORTH BOULEVARD | INJURY COLLISION

A two-vehicle crash was reported on southbound Wadsworth near Wells Road. Both vehicles reportedly sustained significant front-end damage, and one blocked a left-turn lane. One driver was reportedly transported to a hospital.

2:54 PM | REGIONAL CARJACKING ALERT

Jefferson County dispatch received information concerning a reported armed carjacking involving a black Toyota RAV4. Radio traffic placed the vehicle in the Jewell Avenue and C-470 area after earlier tracking near I-70.

The information appears related to a carjacking initially reported in Denver.

2:41 PM | HIGHWAY 285 AND HIGHWAY 121 | COLLISION

A two-vehicle crash was reported near Highway 285 and Highway 121. A possible head injury was initially mentioned, but subsequent information indicated the vehicles had moved to the shoulder and occupants reported no injuries.

2:30 PM | LAKEWOOD | POSSIBLE EXPLOSION

Emergency crews were dispatched to a report of a possible explosion on First Street in Lakewood. Squad 111 was assigned to investigate. No confirmation of an explosion or resulting damage was included in the available information.

2:26 PM | GENESEE | MOTOR VEHICLE COLLISION

A trooper encountered a crash near the I-70 Exit 253 area by Chief Hosa Road. Lane blocking was reportedly unnecessary at that time, although responding resources remained nearby.

2:11 PM | LAKEWOOD | OVERDOSE RESPONSE WITH CPR

Emergency responders were dispatched to Loma Linda Laundry in the Colfax Avenue area for a reported overdose.

Dispatch information indicated CPR was being performed for a patient with agonal breathing and naloxone was being administered. The patient’s outcome was not available.

Traffic was affected in both directions, with the first lane and HOV lane impacted. A tow truck was on scene, and the second lane was reported open.

DENVER

5:28 PM | DOWNTOWN | DISABLED BUSES

Transit dispatch reported a bus that had become disabled near 18th and Larimer streets was restarted and moved toward Union Station.

A second bus was reportedly causing a traffic obstruction in the area.

5:02 PM | 13TH AND CHAMPA | JUVENILE ASSAULT REPORT

5:00 PM | 38TH AVENUE AREA | VEHICLE CRASH

4:51 PM | TRANSIT PLATFORM | DISTURBANCE

4:45 PM | WADSWORTH BOULEVARD | BUS PASSENGER ASSAULT

4:34 PM | 28TH AND LAWRENCE | WEAPONS COMPLAINT

4:29 PM | I-25 NEAR COLFAX | COLLISION

A crash on northbound I-25 just south of Colfax temporarily closed the right lane.

Later dispatch updates indicated the vehicle had been removed from the highway and additional traffic control was no longer necessary.

4:07 PM | LARIMER AND 11TH | BUS STRIKES OBJECT

Transit radio communications reported a bus missed a detour near 11th and Larimer streets and apparently struck a pole or concrete traffic barrier. The extent of the damage was not immediately established.

4:03 PM | COLFAX AND JOSEPHINE | GUN REPORTED

Dispatch received a report of a person allegedly pointing a small handgun at passing vehicles near East Colfax Avenue and Josephine Street.

No injuries or arrests were confirmed in the available information.

3:21 PM | NORTH WHEELING STREET | AGGRESSIVE DOGS

An officer requested assistance after two dogs, described in the initial report as pit bulls, allegedly broke through a fence and behaved aggressively toward people.

3:12 PM | JOHNSON HABITAT PARK | INJURED RACCOON

A caller reported a raccoon appearing severely injured or ill and barely moving at Johnson Habitat Park, 610 South Jason Street.

An officer was dispatched to investigate.

2:53 PM | SLOAN’S LAKE PARK | MOTORCYCLE COMPLAINT

A caller reported a juvenile riding a motorcycle on a park footpath near West 17th Avenue and Wolff Street.

A park ranger was requested to investigate.

2:51 PM | 4TH AND COLORADO | POSSIBLE COERCION

A bus operator reported a concerning interaction between a man and woman near East Fourth Avenue and Colorado Boulevard.

According to the report, the woman appeared frightened, and the man was yelling at her. The two repeatedly boarded and exited the bus before walking toward a vehicle.

Transit police were requested to respond and review surveillance footage.

2:43 PM | NORTH LOGAN STREET | ARMED CARJACKING

A black Toyota RAV4 was reportedly stolen at gunpoint by two suspects near North Logan Street.

One suspect was reportedly armed with a handgun.

Dispatch communications indicated a phone inside the vehicle was providing location information, initially placing it near East 40th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard.
