text:
Elon Daily 20261108

① 🚀 NASA Selects Starship for a 2028 Lunar Communications Mission

NASA has announced a new round of lunar infrastructure procurement, with SpaceX selected as one of the companies eligible to compete under the CLPS 2 framework, worth up to $10 billion.

Starship is also expected to support a 2028 demonstration involving the deployment of communications satellites in cislunar space.

Importantly, the $10 billion represents the combined ceiling for multiple contractors—not a contract awarded to SpaceX.

The bigger picture: Starship’s potential commercial role is expanding beyond satellite launches and lunar landings into building infrastructure between Earth and the Moon.

② 🚕 Tesla Plans Cybercab Efficiency Improvements and More Color Options

Reports on November 8 suggest Tesla is working on improving Cybercab’s energy efficiency while expanding its available color options.

Specific efficiency gains and implementation timelines have not been disclosed.

But Cybercab’s biggest challenge isn’t its color palette or energy consumption.

It’s whether Tesla can achieve reliable, scalable unsupervised FSD—and whether real-world Robotaxi demand can absorb its planned production capacity.

Without sufficient deployment, expanding production risks creating another costly mismatch between manufacturing capacity and actual demand.

③ 🤖 Musk Responds to Grok Bot Usage-Limit Complaints

A subscriber paying $200 per month reported exhausting their Grok Bot usage allowance in approximately 14 hours.

Musk responded on November 8, saying the team is working to improve token efficiency and intelligence.

The incident highlights a fundamental challenge in commercializing AI agents.

Complex, continuously running tasks can consume enormous computing resources. Even premium subscriptions don’t necessarily translate into unlimited usage.

Reducing inference costs per completed task will be critical to Grok’s long-term competitiveness and profitability.

④ 📱 Tesla Robotaxi App Introduces Vehicle Comparison Features

A demonstration of Robotaxi App version 26.11.0, shared on November 7, shows riders comparing Cybercab and Model Y options based on pricing, estimated arrival times, and vehicle availability.

The feature could improve the rider experience while giving Tesla greater flexibility in managing a mixed Robotaxi fleet.

It may also help passengers make more informed choices between different vehicle types.

However, Tesla has not officially confirmed the full rollout scope of these features.

⑤ 📡 Starlink Helps Support Mountain Rescue in Kazakhstan

On November 8, Musk reposted a report describing how Starlink helped rescue teams establish communications with five stranded people in a mountainous region of Kazakhstan.

The incident offers another example of Starlink’s potential value in remote areas where traditional cellular networks are unavailable.

Beyond consumer broadband, emergency communications and disaster response remain important real-world applications for satellite connectivity.

⑥ 🔥 Musk Condemns Dave Chappelle Over Charlie Kirk Assassination Remarks

On November 8, Musk reposted Benny Johnson’s criticism of comedian Dave Chappelle following controversial remarks about Charlie Kirk’s assassination during a performance at Madison Square Garden.

Musk wrote:

“Shame, shame, shame on Chappelle.”

According to media reports, Chappelle suggested during his performance that he had felt better since Kirk’s assassination.

Johnson pointed out that Kirk had publicly defended Chappelle after the comedian was attacked onstage in 2022.

Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, also publicly criticized the remarks.

The controversy has reignited debate over political violence, the boundaries of comedy, and America’s deepening cultural divisions.

Musk’s public condemnation has brought even greater attention to the controversy.

text:
Fair question. I pulled the filings, and the answer surprised me.

Medi-Cal DSH: since 2024 UCLA has taken Global Payment Program money instead. GPP replaces DSH for public systems that join it, and state law makes a UC hospital in GPP ineligible for Medi-Cal DSH. DHCS shows GPP payments to UCLA of $45.1M for 2024 and $34.8M paid so far for 2025. The Grok figure upthread is right. One catch: GPP pays for care to the uninsured, not Medi-Cal.

Medicare DSH: the cost reports for the year ending June 2025 show $8.5M for Ronald Reagan and $3.0M for Santa Monica, plus about $3.0M and $1.5M in uncompensated care payments. The two hospitals had about $4.1B in net patient revenue.

340B: both qualify as state government hospitals, and their Medicare DSH adjustment percentages, which are calculated from Medicaid and Medicare SSI patient days, came in at 25.7% and 15.4% against an 11.75% bar. No contract is needed. UCLA reports $133.4M in 340B savings for FY2024, so nine figures is right.

So losing one contract doesn't end eligibility, but Medi-Cal volume is what feeds that percentage, and Santa Monica has much less room than Reagan. The 340B statute doesn't say how savings must be spent. The SUSTAIN 340B Act in the Senate would make hospitals report it.

What lapsed on June 30 was one Medi-Cal specialty contract with Health Care LA for about 9,000 patients. UCLA says it offered an extension and still contracts with the state's largest Medi-Cal plan and several others, while Health Care LA says UCLA declined to renegotiate and just wanted out. Medi-Cal was about 15% of UCLA's net patient revenue last year, against about 22% at each of the other four UC systems. UCLA disputes that comparison because its county hospital work isn't counted.

Ed is right that Medi-Cal pays below cost, and UCLA itself cites rising denials. Brad is right that a public hospital that earns these programs on its low-income share should be held to a higher bar. Both can be true. We'll get further on this working together.

text:
Pope Leo XIV’s new encyclical on artificial intelligence includes a statement that warrants serious attention from technologists and policymakers: “Technology is never neutral.” Magnifica Humanitas (“Magnificent Humanity”) is a clarion call to all people to act with courage and solidarity as we enter an age already being transformed by artificial intelligence, the greatest change in human life since the Industrial Revolution. As the pope says, the choice before us—the choice AI presents—is one between the Tower of Babel and the rebuilding of our common humanity. 

In the biblical story of the Tower of Babel, humans sought to build a massive structure that reached all the way to Heaven, only to have their project thwarted when God made those involved unable to understand one another. It was a pursuit fixated on relentless growth, divorced from any concern about God’s commandments or the human cost. It resulted in failure and atomization.

The Book of Nehemiah, however, offers a contrasting narrative, in which the rebuilding of Jerusalem after a period of violence and displacement becomes an opportunity for humanity to show its collaborative resilience. As the encyclical puts it, “The city is reborn, not through the initiative of one man, but through the shared responsibility of all: men, women, priests, artisans, heads of households and young people all play a part. It is an undertaking with God at the center, which rebuilds relationships before rebuilding with stones.” 

Is there any question which road we are currently barreling down? And can there be any doubt which we would do well to walk together? 

We are both Catholics, members of religious communities and longtime advocates within the movement for socially responsible investment. Of particular interest to us and that movement is Pope Leo’s point that AI is not some force of nature or hyperrational, ineffable entity. Instead, he reminds us, AI is ultimately another commercial product, one emerging at a point in history when excessive power over commerce and the wider society has amassed in a vanishingly small number of hands. 

It’s a powerful message. It’s also one that institutional investors have been acting on for years. This encyclical doesn’t break new ground so much as ratify a governance effort that’s already underway, led not by states or international bodies but by shareholders. When governments fail to meaningfully regulate, and corporations cannot be trusted to do what is beneficial beyond their own bottom line, people in society still have the power to set us on the right path, and indeed have the duty to do so. 

Around the world, AI systems are being deployed at scale with remarkably little institutional oversight. There is no AI safety board. The US Federal Trade Commission has jurisdiction over unfair practices but limited authority over algorithmic design. The National Institute of Standards and Technology publishes guidance that most companies ignore. The EU AI Act is partially in force but addresses only a sliver of the deployment surface.

Institutional investors have stepped into this vacuum. Coalitions including the membership of the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility, representing investors managing over $4 trillion in assets, have spent the past several proxy seasons filing resolutions demanding transparency, risk assessment, and accountability around AI deployment. Secular institutional investors have joined them, treating AI governance failures as material business risks.

Shareholders have called tech giants including Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Palantir, and Uber to account and demanded that AI not be used for acts of violence or other violations of human rights. The importance of this aspect of corporate governance was highlighted tragically in the opening hours of the war against Iran, when AI was used to help identify targets for thousands of missile strikes that killed hundreds of people.  

Investors have also challenged executives at CVS and UnitedHealth Group to ensure that AI not be used to undermine the well-being of patients and quality of health care across the United States. 

At companies including Meta and Microsoft, shareholders have decried the environmental impact of AI data centers, which consume vast amounts of energy and precious water resources, and in turn can emit large amounts of greenhouse gases. 

Within creative industries, investors have challenged the leadership at companies like Disney, Netflix, and Warner Bros. to demand transparency about the ways they are using AI and to defend the inimitable human element in storytelling. 

Soon, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Grok all set to enter the public markets, we will be able to exert similar influence over what are now all privately held entities.

These actions by concerned investors not only call out misdeeds but hold fast to an immutable truth: that it is wrong to use technology to kill, harm, or oppress people. Every human being has a right to safe and effective health care and the opportunity to earn a dignified living. The stories we tell each other matter and require the human creative spark. 

Investor advocates hail from a range of faith traditions. Some have no formal religious faith. Yet in their informed and tenacious advocacy, all these people echo the calls embedded within Pope Leo’s encyclical and act on its declaration that “it is essential that the use of AI, especially when it touches on public goods and fundamental rights, be guided by clear criteria and effective oversight.” 

Encyclicals mark time. A century from now, how will we be remembered for how we met this moment? Will we be seen as having been too timid or shortsighted to prevent a small group of unfathomably wealthy and self-interested people from seizing ever greater control over the human family’s shared destiny? 

Or will the years ahead be remembered as a turning point that helped us rebuild our common humanity? Let this be a time when people of good will and diverse talents come together through their own magnificent humanity to build a future that honors our Creator.

Father Séamus Finn, OMI, is a global leader in faith-based and socially responsible investing and a priest of the Oblates of Mary Immaculate, a missionary religious congregation.

Sister Susan Francois is the assistant congregation leader and congregation treasurer for the Sisters of St. Joseph of Peace.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misstated the amount under management by the membership of the Interfaith Center on Corporate Responsibility.

text:
Anthropic’s IPO bankers are considering raising its $70–$78 share price range following strong investor demand, potentially lifting its valuation above $1.5T and combined fundraising beyond $100B, according to the Financial Times.

•IPO Pricing: 
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are weighing an increase after strong interest during Tuesday’s roadshow. The original range values Anthropic at $1.26T–$1.41T on a fully diluted basis, with a listing expected next week.

•Fundraising: 
The IPO targets up to $64B, plus nearly $10B through an over-allotment option and $26B in private investments from partners including Google ($GOOGL), Nvidia ($NVDA) and Microsoft ($MSFT). Backers say securing capital for expansion now takes priority over pursuing a higher valuation.

•AI Spending: 
Anthropic plans approximately $900B in future computing and infrastructure spending. Its annualized revenue run rate reached $81B in October, while actual Q3 revenue totaled $17B.

•Investor Demand: 
A brokerage is offering up to $500M in allocated shares at a 4% premium to the final IPO price. Another investor is marketing $1.25B through an SPV at a $1.5T valuation. Anthropic warns that certain secondary-market offers will not be recognized.

•Valuation Risks: 
Earlier $2T IPO ambitions moderated amid AI spending concerns and a recent $3.2T tech selloff. Morningstar estimates fair equity value at $1.7T, with a potential range of $500B–$3T depending on AI adoption.

text:
Sometimes communications are very direct confirmations meant for anons. 

But every now and again— have you ever noticed that President Trump, the White House, or certain military-affiliated accounts or patriots post something that looks oddly out of place—strange misspellings, unusual capitalization, weird numbers, or a statement that doesn’t quite fit the moment?

This is a long-standing form of low-tech communication used by Trump and patriots aligned with him. Sometimes the audience is the public; sometimes it’s specific operators or insiders. 

What I am describing are steganographic or cryptographic signaling.

In these systems, the surface post is ordinary enough to be deniable. The real information is carried by deliberate “errors” or markers that only people with a shared key can read. A misspelling, a specific number, an odd timestamp, or a particular word order acts as a flag. 

Only Recipients who possess the codebook know which markers correspond to which pre-arranged meanings or actions. Think of it as a map and legend that only certain people have. 

Suppose you and a small group of patriots have agreed in advance that when a post contains the specific misspelling “Perade,” the extra “e” is the trigger. That single letter, combined with the time of posting or another agreed signal, tells you which action to take. Everyone else sees a typo. They see an instruction.

This approach offers strong plausible deniability and works over public channels that may be monitored. 

It doesn’t require encrypted apps, secure phones, or special equipment—just a pre-shared understanding and the ability to post or notice a post. 

In environments where conventional communications could be compromised, the method is simple, low-signature, and difficult to prove as intentional after the fact.

Military and intelligence organizations have used similar techniques for decades: open-source signaling, one-time codebooks, and steganographic markers embedded in routine traffic. 

The same principle is definitely being applied within the Trump admin. And Those holding the key see coordinated direction.

But always remember the very obvious comms of reassurance meant for us— such as “PATRIOTS IN CONTROL”

text:
✨ When applying the traditional tilak on the brother's forehead, sisters can chant these powerful mantras to invoke divine blessings for his health, longevity, and protection.

1. The Traditional Bhai Dooj Mantra:
This is the most popular mantra, referencing the legendary story of Yamuna and her brother Yama (the God of Death).

गंगा पूजे यमुना को, यमी पूजे यमराज को।
सुभद्रा पूजे कृष्ण को, गंगा यमुना नीर बहे, मेरे भाई की आयु बढ़े।
• Transliteration: Ganga pooje Yamuna ko, Yami pooje Yamraj ko. Subhadra pooje Krishna ko, Ganga Yamuna neer bahe, mere bhai ki aayu badhe.
• Meaning: Just as the holy river Ganga worships the Yamuna, and Yami worships Her brother Yamraj, and Subhadra worships Her brother Lord Sri Krishna—may my brother's life and longevity flow continuously like the holy waters of the Ganga and Yamuna.

2. The Bhai Phonta Mantra (Bengali Tradition):
If you follow the Eastern/Bengali tradition, this rhyming verse is chanted while using the little finger to apply sandalwood paste and kajal.

ভাইয়ের কপালে দিলাম ফোঁটা, যম দুয়ারে পড়লো কাঁটা।
যমুনা দেয় যমকে ফোঁটা, আমি দিই আমার ভাইকে ফোঁটা।
যমুনার হাতে ফোঁটা খেয়ে যম হল চিরজীবী, আমার হাতে ফোঁটা পেয়ে আমার ভাই হোক দীর্ঘজীবী
• Transliteration: Bhai-er kopale dilam phonta, Jom duyare porlo kanta.
Jomuna dey Jom-ke phonta, Ami di-ee amar bhai-ke phonta.
Jomunar hate phonta kheye Jom holo chirojibi, Amar hate phonta peye amar bhai hok dirghojibi.
• Meaning: I place this mark upon my brother's forehead, thereby casting a thorn across the door of Death. Just as Yamuna gave a mark to Yama, I give this mark to my brother. As Yama is immortal, may my brother become immortal too.

3. The Vedic Blessing Mantra:
For a traditional Vedic ritual, you can chant this Sanskrit shloka while applying the tilak and offering akshat (unbroken rice grains).

भ्रातस्तवानुजाताहं भुंक्ष्व भक्तमिदं शुभम्।
प्रीतये यमराजस्य यमुनाया विशेषतः॥
• Transliteration: Bhratastavanujataham bhunkshva bhaktamidam shubham. Preetaye yamarajasya yamunaya visheshatah.
• Meaning: O brother, I, your sister, lovingly offer you this auspicious meal. May this ritual bring joy and satisfaction to Lord Yamraj and Goddess Yamuna, and may they bless you with protection.

text:
💠 Bhai Dooj (also known as Bhai Tika, Bhau Beej, or Bhai Phonta) is a Hindu festival celebrating the sacred bond between brothers and sisters, observed on the second lunar day of the bright fortnight (Shukla Paksha) in the holy month of Kartik ✨

✨ Details & Significance:
Date: Celebrated two days after Diwali (in 2026, it falls on November 11).
Main Ritual: Sisters apply a ceremonial tilak (vermilion, sandalwood, or kajal) on their brothers' foreheads, perform aarti, and pray for their long, healthy, and prosperous lives.
Reciprocation: Brothers offer gifts, sweets, and a lifelong promise to protect and support their sisters.
Other Names: Known as Yama Dwitiya, because it marks the day the God of Death visited his sister.

✨ The Legend:
Yama and Yamuna: According to Hindu traditions, Lord Yama (the God of Death) visited his sister, Goddess Yamuna, on this day. Devi Yamuna welcomed him with a warm meal, applied a tilak, and performed aarti.
The Divine Boon: Deeply moved by Her genuine affection and hospitality, Yama declared that any brother who receives a tilak and aarti from his sister on this day will be protected from untimely danger and granted a long, blessed life.

✨ Unique Regional Traditions:-

Bihar & Eastern Uttar Pradesh: Known as Yama Dwitiya, where sisters traditionally scold or hurl symbolic curses at their brothers (pricking their own tongues with a thorn as penance) to ward off any evil eye or danger from Yama.

West Bengal (Bhai Phonta): Sisters observe a fast until the ritual is completed, applying a phonta made of sandalwood paste, kajal, and ghee on the brother's forehead while chanting mantras for his safety.

Maharashtra & Goa (Bhau Beej): The brother sits inside a square drawn on the floor with rice flour and must symbolically bite into a bitter fruit called Karith before the tilak ceremony takes place.

✨ For Bhai Dooj, the most auspicious time (Shubh Muhurat) to perform the traditional tilak ceremony is during the Aparahna (afternoon) period.

Because the Dwitiya Tithi concludes at 3:53 PM, the primary ritual window is short.

National Muhurat (New Delhi):-
Auspicious Time Window: 01:10 PM to 03:20 PM
Duration: 2 Hours 10 Mins

Dwitiya Tithi End Time: 03:53 PM
Rituals must finish before this time.

Alternative Morning Timings (Yoga & Choghadiya):-
If you cannot perform the ceremony in the afternoon, astrologers note a highly auspicious morning window driven by the Sarvartha Siddhi Yoga:
Morning Window: 06:40 AM to 11:38 AM
Best Choghadiya Periods: Labh (06:40 AM – 08:01 AM) and Amrit (08:01 AM – 09:23 AM). 

⚠️ Hours to Avoid (Rahu Kaal):-
Sisters are strongly advised not to perform the tilak during Rahu Kaal, which runs from 12:05 PM to 01:27 PM, as it is considered inauspicious.

text:
There is homelessness, but its hidden because  of the deep shame people feel, in a country in which harmony of the many over runs the need of the individual.

Marginalized youth, code word often for  children escaping abuse at home. They can't get an apartment of their own because parents refuse to give them the ID info compulsory for just about everything in life. So the boys become pimps, girls the products. They sleep in railway stations, in doorways, and when they scrap enough together,  a night in a "affordable" hotel.

Then we have the working poor. People who work as salary men (women called it too) with all the crazy hours demanded by Japanese companies, who will often pay an Internet Cafe which is "affordable housing"  until the end of the month when money gets tight. $13-27 will get you a night on a mattress, free internet and occasionally a shower. The $27 cafes often have a kitchens  with soup, comfort foods along with rice, ramen, coffee, tea or juice. If you're lucky you can access a capsule hotel. $35 - 55 up to $100 on a weekend will let you sleep in relative luxury. 

We also have the issue of hikomori - people who withdraw from life and stay only in their rooms. Often they are protected and supported by their parents. But the parents eventually die and their child has no right to keep living in the family home, and no way to support themselves.  Because of the shame involved with mental illness, there is a resistance to reaching out for medical help or talk therapy, so these people are almost in suspended animation. 

The culture in many Asian countries is one where you do not share living spaces with non family, which is a possible explanation as to working adults having no where to live. No shared flats. And getting a parents signature as a guarantor for teens to rent an apartment adds yet another twist to the mess.

Here is a list of JUST the papers required to rent an apartment. 

• Passport and Residence Card (Zairyu Card) to prove your legal identity and status in Japan.
• Certificate of Employment or Job Offer Letter (or a school acceptance letter for students) to prove your activity in the country.
• Proof of Income such as recent pay slips or tax certificates; landlords and guarantor companies generally look for a monthly income.
• Emergency Contact Information and a designated local phone number or bank account.
• Inkan / Hanko (Personal Seal) and an Inkan Shomeisho (Seal Registration Certificate), though some modern agencies may accept a standard signature.

Moving into a standard Tokyo apartment requires a substantial initial payment, typically totaling 4 to 6 months' rent. Poorer, less desirable area can cost an average of $650 a month. That's $3900  for just the deposit for an apartment.

• Security Deposit (Shikikin): 1 to 2 months' rent (held for damages or cleaning upon moving out).
• Key Money (Reikin): 0 to 2 months' rent (a non-refundable "thank-you" gift to the landlord)
• Brokerage Fee (Chukai Tesuryo): 1 month's rent plus consumption tax paid to the real estate agent.
• Advance Rent: The first full month's (and sometimes pro-rated current month's) base rent and management fee.
• Fire & Liability Insurance: Standard annual or multi-year property insurance coverage.
• Key Replacement / Lock-Change Fee: A one-time payment to change locks

None of these people are counted as homeless by the government because on paper they don't exist officially.

Indeed there are social housing options, but the paperwork requirements remains the same. There are homes being offered in rural areas of the country at minimal cost, but employment options are very limited.

 I completely adore the country, culture, food, the Japanese people. I'd joyfully move there if I had the means, so I don't share this piece as an attack, but rather a reality check for people making sweeping statements of how very perfect this country is. It is a country that faces its own deep societal issues and problems.

text:
It’s time once again to remind the public that Steve Bannon comes up 2777 times in the Epstein files.  

The records show a close, familiar, and ongoing personal/professional relationship after Bannon left the Trump White House. 

Bannon advised Epstein on handling public scrutiny of his criminal history (including the 2008 Florida plea deal involving a minor), media coverage, legal responses, and public image. He described the attention as a “sophisticated op,” counseled against responding in ways that would amplify coverage, and suggested steps like “push back on the lies; then crush the pedo/trafficking narrative; then rebuild your image as philanthropist.” They discussed crisis communications, op-eds, interviews, and a film project.

They planned extensive filming (Bannon has publicly said he has roughly 15 hours of footage, with some video later released by DOJ). This included discussions of filming on Epstein’s island. Messages reference media training and, in some reports, a possible Kovel agreement (to extend attorney-client privilege). Bannon has framed the project as a documentary that would expose Epstein; contemporary reporting and some messages describe elements of image rehabilitation.

Epstein helped arrange or advise on Bannon’s travel (e.g., alternative flights after the Oxford Union speech was delayed by protests, charters). Epstein joked about being “the most highly paid travel agent in history” with “Massages. Not Included.”

Bannon sought Epstein’s contacts, advice, and potential funding support for right-wing/populist efforts in Europe (references to figures such as Matteo Salvini and Marine Le Pen). Epstein offered introductions and strategic suggestions; they also discussed broader geopolitics and U.S. politics.

Messages include banter, scheduling (e.g., a February 2019 breakfast), discussions of Trump, and mutual updates. Contact continued until around July 6, 2019—the day of Epstein’s arrest—when Epstein messaged “All canceled.”

房迷 From Me Daily 11/10/2026

- 朋友跟我說，麥當勞有McRib在賣，昨天吃了一發
- 還說服兩個兒子都吃McRib，廣受好評，這段時間可以吃一下
- 當然這是重組肉，沒有肋排肉，但是畢竟都吃麥當勞了，不講究
- 我是覺得重鹹、重甜、重醬汁，口感不差
- 美國人不習慣吃豬肉，所以1985年後就不在常態菜單，限定回歸反而夯
- McRib通常在10-11月，豬肉價格低的時候出現
- 好像說豬隻在夏季大量增肥，10-11月進入屠宰高峰期，價格最低
- 麥當勞的體量剛好進場採購，吃膩牛肉漢堡也可以剛好吃一下豬肉漢堡
- Homestyle Roll麵包也是不同口感，吃起來messy不適合開車吃就是了
- 我是覺得美國連鎖，還是麥當勞跟星巴克最厲害
- 不是說東西好吃那種厲害，就是又貴又難吃，卻老是不爭氣地去送錢

- 今天聽國大收討論美國人民反對AI，反觀中國人民擁抱AI
- 水電費這種表面理由，只是比較好敘事，法規面也容易實作，其實不是重點
- 喜惡這種事情，我還是比較看人性
- 美國人日子過得舒服，自然比較害怕失去，不想改變現狀
- 現在好好的，也沒感覺AI能給什麼好處，還可能取代工作，要重新學新技能
- 事實上看到的是分配不平均，除了AI天龍人、買進AI股的人，到底誰有好處了
- 我在房市看的壞處更多，利率太高，大家買不起房，影響的人民更多
- 而且各種工人與建材，都因為蓋資料中心搶資源，大幅漲價
- 中國人日子本來就苦，想的是彎道超車，看到的是新的機會
- 人民本來就喜歡卷，競爭是日常，不怕辛苦
- 分配不平均更是沒有在怕，出生看到的就是不平均，習慣了吃苦
- 研究上看，中國人也怕工作被取代，但他們習慣了各種變化
- 過去幾十年，科技對中國一直是淨利多，自然對下一個科技也樂觀
- 這是我個人想法，我自己是支持AI的，上面是分析大量人民想法，不是我的

- 至於AI發展，到底對美國比較好，還是對中國比較好，我不知道
- 中國面臨嚴重的人口老化問題，是非常需要AI解救的
- 美國有很多法規、制度、基建上的問題，即使有AI，後面摩擦力很大
- 從資本市場角度看，當然對美國是比較好的，這個沒疑問
- 但我會覺得，沒有AI，美國會好好的，但是中國會完蛋
- 使用AI上，極權政府比民主政府更能施力，用的效果更好(方向不一定好)
- 我還是會回到製造業，昨天說過了，物理AI是中國的天下
- 國家強弱最終也要回到軍事，我沒有那麼確定，發展AI對美中競爭有利
- 當然，我認同對任何國家，發展AI都比較好，而且那個好可能超越彼此的差距

- $ANT如期上市，蠻多人應該會參與IPO購買
- 估值現在看起來$1.1-1.4T，比之前喊到的$2T差了不少
- 從現在公開市場AI下殺估值的比例來看，也是合理
- 融資最多$64B左右，股價大概$70-$78之間
- 各大雲業者跟AI基礎建設公司，很多在IPO買進$ANT股票，高達$26B
- Dario説癌症、阿茲海默、心臟病、精神疾病，不到十年會成為過去
- AI可以解決人類的難題，開創奇蹟時代
- 好險這次他應該沒說，人類自己不到十年也會成為過去
- TAM寫到$40T+
- 今天發表的Claude Whiteboards跟Claude Sheets，我覺得也蠻好的
- 2024/11-2025/07拿的offer，包裹都是用一股$5.61算的
- 資深工程師『每年』$250k的股票，上市後可以變成$3.3M
- 時間只要大概兩年，是史上最快造富，這是為什麼你要來矽谷工作
- $ANT的員工手持~$216B的股票(一股算$78)，總共5300人
- 還有$160B股票池，發給未來進來的員工

- 十月CPI通膨沒有YoY數據，因為去年這時候政府關門
- CPI MoM +0.4%，預期+0.3%，前值+0.6%
- Core CPI MoM +0.3%，預期+0.2%，前值+0.3%
- 通膨還是偏高，這是很正常的，中東戰爭+關稅戰+AI擴張
- 商品跟服務的價格壓力都很廣，企業在把成本轉嫁給消費者
- 經濟學家估計整體年通膨大概還在high 3%
- shelter MoM +0.3%，佔整體漲幅超過30%，佔Core CPI超過40%
- 12月Fed升息幾乎是肯定的，主要是把去年底的預防性降息收回來
- 2027年初再升息的機率也變高，對房貸不利
- Fed理事Christopher Wallace說12月可以考慮升2碼
- 他是在CPI數據以前說的，即使通膨數據好也要加1碼，不好就2碼
- Dallas Fed總裁Lorie Logan也說，冬天要更快加息，至少需要再加2碼
- 主要就業市場很好，數據上幾乎沒什麼好理由讓Fed不加息
- 如果就是再加息2碼，但是結束伊朗戰爭，我覺得還可以穩住

NAR NXT 2026會議
- 美國房市累積了相當大的壓抑需求
- 只要利率降、庫存變好、信心回來，這些需求就會放出來
- 跟2000年比，美國人口從2.81億變3.5億，薪資工作從1.32億變1.59億
- 但今年成屋銷售只有4M左右，2000年是5.2M
- 人變多、工作變多、財富變多，房子卻賣得更少，就是被利率卡住
- 可負擔性很難，但收入在漲，如果利率降下來，被放出來的需求會很可觀
- 供給面上，銷售變慢，庫存就上來了，months' supply是2015年以來最高
- 賣家要面對現實，現在買家很艱難，價格沒有正確預期會很難賣
- 首購族不只買不起房，房租、學貸都壓力大，現在連托育費用也越來越重
- 根據數據，23%的房仲每天用AI，25%每週用，31%偶爾試試
- 只有12%說不用也不打算用，2025年還沒試過AI的有32%
- AI裡有相當多房子相關事實都還是錯的，問題是客戶都照樣用
- 買家現在看房，都會帶著AI給的印象，房仲專業度更重要

Redfin數據
- 9月全美condo賣家比買家多123%(去年95.5%)，是2013年有紀錄以來差距最大
- 2021/09疫情搶房的時候，condo賣家還比買家少25.1%
- 五年後買家少了54%，賣家多了36%，完全反過來
- 不過Redfin這個賣家/買家數量的算法，產業內不認同的很多(包括我)
- 但同樣一個數據，在不同時間點的趨勢，是有可比性的
- 保險跟HOA一直漲，condo持有成本越來越高
- Florida跟Texas因為颶風跟天災，保險貴得更誇張
- 其實我認為，保險跟持有成本，獨棟一樣在增加，只是不會換成每月的數字
- 當然獨棟有更多的自由度，絕對是真的
- 全美condo中位成交價跌0.8%到$339k，五個月來第一次YoY下跌
- 9月賣掉的condo大概37%有降價，五年前疫情時只有16%
- 9月賣掉的condo平均上市63天才進合約，五年前是35天
- 全美的condo都超慘，尤其sun belt，還有新建案在增加供給
- 舊金山則是平衡市場，condo 9月中位成交價YoY +20%，將近$1.2M
- 舊金山需求回來跟AI熱潮有關，高薪的人進來就開始買房
- 灣區其他地方就沒這麼熱，我第一線看到的，是condo真的完蛋了

===

不管吃什麼，都先按讚來一發，房迷按讚不搞限定回歸，追求每天無止盡按讚，畢竟我們不是豬隻，每天都有最高價值，我是覺得房迷連載，還是每天來按讚的人最厲害，趕快爭氣點加入

text:
1564. The Huguenots attempt settlement in Florida on the St. John’s River.

Huguenot explorer Rene Goulaine de Laudonniere left France in the spring of 1564, carrying Huguenot Protestants seeking refuge amid the religious wars tearing France apart. They reached the mouth of the St. Johns River and chose a site on a bluff, they began building Fort Caroline, a triangular wooden fort named after King Charles IX.

Chief Saturiwa and his people, the Timucua, came out to meet them. Saturiwa already knew the French from Ribault’s visit two years earlier. He greeted Laudonniere, led him to the stone column Ribault had planted in 1562. 

The Timucua had turned it into a sacred object of veneration. Rather than viewing it as a territorial marker, the Timucua used it in their spiritual practices, decorating it with leafy wreaths, garlands, and fruits from their harvest.

They exchanged gifts. Saturiwa offered silver for metal tools, knives, and small trade goods. Saturiwa then took Laudonniere by the hand and proposed an alliance. He described his enemies, the Utina, who lived farther up the river and promised riches if the French fought with them. Saturiwa’s people helped build Fort Caroline, and for a short time they worked side by side, shared food, all seemed well.

Then the alliance fell apart, Saturiwa wanted the French to send soldiers to his aid to fight the Utina, but Laudonniere decided not to risk the lives of his men. Saturiwa felt betrayed by this, and grew cold. As French stores dwindled, his men were forced to take food from nearby villages. Later, Laudonniere himself led a party upriver, seized the Utina Chief, and held him hostage to force the delivery of supplies.

By the summer of 1565 the French were isolated, short of food, and no longer trusted by the locals. The French expected resupply from home, but none came, the colony ran short of food, sickness spread. Through the winter and spring of 1565 the colonists grew weaker. By midsummer, Laudonniere was preparing to abandon the site. 

Then, when all seemed lost, Jean Ribault arrived from France with hundreds of settlers, and boatloads of supplies. The settlement was saved, all seemed well once again. 

But around the same time of Ribault’s arrival, the Spanish under Pedro Menendez also reached Florida with orders to expel the Protestant Heretics. He established a base at what became St. Augustine Florida, and prepared to attack Fort Caroline.

When the Spanish attacked in September, Chief Saturiwa and the Timucua stayed out of the fight. In the first battle between European powers in the New World, Menendez marched his men overland through thick woods in the rain, and attacked Fort Caroline on the morning of September 20, 1565.

The garrison was caught by surprise, most of the men inside were killed, women and children were spared and some, including Laudonniere, escaped to ships and eventually returned to France. The Spanish renamed Fort Caroline to Fort San Mateo.

Ribault moved to strike the Spanish, but his ships were scattered in a storm. Ribault and several hundred of his men, shipwrecked, and later surrendered to the Spanish under promise of mercy, but Menendez had a majority of them executed anyway, as heretics. 

The French colony was extinguished after a little more than a year. A later French raid in 1568 destroyed the newly named Spanish garrison at San Mateo. Saturiwa even joined the French, happy to burn down the fort, and France never rebuilt another settlement in Florida after that.

The site of Fort Caroline has never been found. It was one of the earliest sustained colonial attempts in the present day United States and the beginning of major clashes between European factions vying for power on the continent.

Below is a 16th-century engraving depicting French explorer Rene Goulaine de Laudonniere and Athore (son of Chief Saturiwa) visiting the stone column erected by Jean Ribault in Florida, by Jacques le Moyne des Morgues.

text:
1562. The Huguenots attempt a settlement on the coast of South Carolina.

By the early 1560s Protestantism (mainly Calvinism) had spread in French society, reforming the Church of France. The crown, under the young King Charles IX and his mother Catherine de’ Medici, initially tolerated the reform, but Catholics, led by the powerful Guise family, opposed it.

The First French War of Religion began in March 1562 after a Protestant congregation was ambushed during worship, dozens were killed. Protestants were called to arms and Catholic nobles raised forces in the name of the king, triggering an open civil war.

The word Huguenot was originally a nickname applied to Protestants by Catholics in France, its exact origin is uncertain. The term was already circulating before the outbreak of the war in 1562. Over time the word became the standard term for French Reformed Protestants.

Gaspard de Coligny, Admiral of France and powerful Huguenot noble, promoted overseas colonies in the New World to create a safe haven to worship. He selected a skilled sailor, Jean Ribault, to lead an expedition to claim territory for France (against Spanish interests) and provide a possible refuge for the Huguenot’s.

Ribault, an expert navigator, left France in mid-February and sighted the Florida coast on May 1, 1562, they entered the St. Johns River (the longest river in Florida) and erected a claim, a stone column engraved with the arms of King Charles IX. 

They sailed north until they discovered a massive natural deep-water sound in what is now Port Royal Harbor in South Carolina. Ribault wrote that they “arrived in one of the fairest harbors and greatest havens in the world, the depth is such that the greatest ships of France may enter.” He named it Port Royal, because of its large size and depth, and cast anchor.

The surrounding woods was full with game, and near Parris Island, Ribault built a small timber fort. He named it Charlesfort after his king, and before returning to France for supplies, he asked for volunteers to remain behind in the strange new land, and many stepped forward. 

On June 11, 1562, Ribault’s ship sailed away, expecting to return within months. Instead he found France already torn by the Wars of Religion, and was detained in England, the promise of relief never arrived.

At Charlesfort, they faced dwindling food stores, a fire that destroyed much of what remained, internal conflict, mutiny, and growing isolation. Lacking shipbuilders and sailors, they decided to abandon the fort. They constructed a rickety boat using local timber, and sails made from their own bedsheets. 

In 1563, they set out across the Atlantic without a compass. Starvation followed, they eventually drew lots and one man was consumed before an English ship rescued the survivors. Spanish forces later found the fort abandoned and burned it. They built their own settlement, Santa Elena, in the same area. 

The 1562 attempt lasted less than a year, but it marked the start of French land claims in the new world and a rivalry with Spain. It also set a pattern of Protestant settlement seeking religious tolerance in North America. Later Huguenot groups arrived in 1685, by the tens of thousands seeking safety from persecution, settling in the British North American colonies. 

Their descendants contributed as merchants, craftsmen, planters, soldiers, and political leaders, especially during the Revolutionary era. Some notable figures and prominent families with Huguenot ancestry include Paul Revere, John Jay, George Washington, Henry Laurens, Alexander Hamilton, Gouverneur Morris and E. I. du Pont.

“Jean Ribault's 1562 arrival at St. Johns River” by Lee Adams.

text:
1541. Coronado, coming from Mexico, reaches the heartland, probably northeastern Kansas.

In the spring of 1541, a conquistador named Francisco Vázquez de Coronado pushed farther north than any previous Spanish expedition. At the same time, on the other side of the continent, De Soto’s expedition was adventuring in Florida, but the two forces never met, and neither had yet reached the heartland, the Great Plains.

The Spanish had little knowledge of the interior, maps of the time left those regions blank. After crossing the Sonoran Desert and the Colorado Plateau, Coronado's army reached the Pueblo villages of present-day New Mexico. Sun-baked adobes marked the limit of what Europeans had seen in the Southwest, but Coronado had heard stories proclaiming cities of gold. 

A captive, a man the Spaniards called “The Turk,” began to tell stories of a great kingdom, Quivira, far to the northeast. A place where even the poorest ate from golden dishes. Coronado listened, the story was impossible to ignore. After a hard winter, supplies were thin, the conquistadors thoughts were filled with gold, so shiny.

In late April the whole expedition left the pueblos and pushed onto the open plains. They travelled for weeks over grass so high it brushed the horses’ bellies, and witnessed the endless herds of shaggy cows, even water that appeared and vanished without warning. 

After finding no kingdoms of gold, low on supplies, Coronado sent the main army back, but he went on with a handful of his best men, a friar named Juan de Padilla, and guides, like the Turk,  who claimed they knew the way to this mysterious kingdom of Quivira.

They rode through rough terrain and by June they found a river, the Arkansas, and followed it northeast. The soil of the land grew darker, and they met the first people of Quivira, ancestors of the Wichita people.

The people of Quivira received the strangers in peace. They were tall, many of them over six feet, marked with tattoos, moving on foot among the buffalo. The houses were straw, not stone. They lived in large villages of beehive-shaped grass lodges along the river, and they grew corn, beans, and squash in fields that stretched farther than the eye could see.

Coronado stayed nearly a month, he walked through the villages, tasted the wild plums and grapes that grew along the streams, and listened for any word of gold, but there was none. The only metal he saw was a piece of copper hanging from a chief’s neck. The people he encountered hunted, farmed and tribes fought each other, the same as every other he had met on his journeys. 

The Turk’s stories had been lies, but Coronado was surprised at the land itself, it was, as he said, “The best I have ever seen for producing all the products of Spain, for besides the land itself being very fat and black, and being well watered by the rivulets and springs and rivers, I found prunes like those of Spain, and nuts and very sweet grapes and mulberries.”

The Turk confessed that he had misled the expedition into dangerous country, to draw the armored strangers out where water was scarce so they would die of thirst. Coronado had him executed before their return.

The Coronado party took a shorter route back across the plains and rejoined the main force by early October. The expedition returned to Mexico in 1542, judged a failure for finding no riches. Friar Juan de Padilla returned the next year as a missionary to Quivira and was killed in 1542, ambushed by rival tribes, widely regarded as the first Christian martyr within the present-day United States. 

“America in the Making: Francisco Vasquez De Coronado” by N. C. Wyeth.

Everyday tools can tell extraordinary stories—especially when they reveal how Appalachian families built, traveled, and made a living.

At Heritage Farm Museum & Village in Huntington, West Virginia, seven themed museum buildings explore the ingenuity behind Appalachian life. Discover changing technology in the Progress Museum, explore the Transportation Museum, and check the schedule for artisan demonstrations that keep traditional skills in practice. The village also offers animal encounters and tractor-drawn wagon rides for a fuller family outing.

Little-known fact: Heritage Farm became West Virginia’s first Smithsonian Affiliate, connecting this locally founded celebration of Appalachian culture with the Smithsonian’s nationwide museum network.

Check the seasonal calendar, then spend a day exploring the tools, craftsmanship, and resourcefulness that helped generations of Appalachian communities thrive.

Night Prayer for November 10, 2026 ~~ Feast of the Dedication of a Church

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

O my God, I adore Thee and thank Thee for all the graces granted me this day. I offer Thee my sleep and all the moments of this night. I place myself and all my loved ones in Thy sacred side and under the mantle of Our Blessed Mother. Let Thy holy angels stand watch and keep us in peace.

YOUR WORD CALLS US: “Know you not that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16)

Forgive any infidelities of this day, when I may have been indifferent to Thy inspirations. Restore in me a docile heart that no longer resists the goad of grace. Come, Holy Spirit, Light of the heart ~~ fill me with sorrow for lost graces and resolve to be faithful tomorrow. Grant me rest free from the sadness and bitterness that come from unfaithfulness as I rest in the Feast of the Dedication of a Church. Amen. 

Prayer inspired by Rev. M. Hamon, S.S., Meditations for All the Days of the Year, 3rd Edition, 1894.

text:
The idea that “the whole of historic Palestine belongs exclusively to Palestinians” and every Jew is just an “illegal settler” waiting to be shipped home is a popular slogan. It is not a description of the historical record.

Jews have lived continuously in the land for roughly 3,000 years, including after the Romans destroyed the Second Temple. Communities remained in Jerusalem, Safed, Tiberias, Hebron, and Galilee through every subsequent ruler. The late-19th-century immigration wave expanded an existing presence; it did not invent one. 
https://t.co/LK2CqD7Ie6

Under Ottoman and British rule, Jews bought land legally. By 1947–48 they legally-owned roughly 6–7.6% of Mandatory Palestine (about 1.7–2 million dunams), mostly purchased from absentee landlords under the 1858 Ottoman land code. Large stretches of the rest—especially the Negev—were state or crown land, not private Arab property. Mandate figures put Jewish ownership around 5.67% in 1945. 
https://t.co/9i656VbVW6

In November 1947 the UN recommended partition (Resolution 181): a Jewish state on ~56% of the land (much of it empty Negev), an Arab state on ~43%, and an internationalized Jerusalem. Jewish leaders accepted it. The Arab Higher Committee and Arab League rejected it and promised to block it by force. Civil war started the next day. 

After Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948, armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq, and Lebanon invaded. The resulting 1949 armistice lines left Israel with more territory than the partition map had assigned. 
https://t.co/VNRGz8QzxW

Late-Mandate population was roughly 1.3–1.4 million Arabs and 600,000–650,000 Jews. “Historic Palestine” in this context is the post-1922 British Mandate territory west of the Jordan. It was never a sovereign Palestinian state. Both peoples have deep ties to the same land; the political question was whether a Jewish state would be permitted to exist next to an Arab one once the Mandate ended. 

The 1947 plan offered exactly that. Its rejection, followed by invasion, produced the war and the borders that followed. Thems the breaks.

There. Some actual history for you, Johnny. Try to keep up.

Consider a citizen who works for forty years, pays taxes faithfully, and dies shortly before retirement. 

He is a tragedy to his family. 

To the pension ledger, he represents obligations that will never come due.

Governments keep accounts. Families bury people.

Americans want timely treatment at a price they can afford. 

Washington offers another interminable argument about capitalism, socialism, Obamacare, and Medicare for All, as though the correct political vocabulary could settle a medical bill.

Meanwhile, expensive care is somebody’s revenue. 

Every dollar saved by a patient is a dollar an established institution may lose. 

Those institutions have every reason to influence the officials who write the rules.

We need not imagine a secret meeting at which anyone proposes making Americans poorer or shortening their lives. 

A system can produce appalling results through perfectly ordinary decisions that protect the people already in power.

Cheaper healthcare already exists. Its expansion threatens established interests.

The question is whether Americans can make their government permit that expansion.

A republic has a serious problem when its citizens must petition their representatives for permission to compete with their representatives’ donors.

text:
Larry Flynt was 55 when he paid $85,000 for one ad in the Washington Post. It offered up to $1 million for proof of "an adulterous sexual encounter" with a member of Congress or a high-ranking official.

76 days later, the man picked to be the next Speaker of the House stood up in the middle of Bill Clinton's impeachment debate and gave it all up.

In the video below, Flynt in January 1999: "I didn't start this. Ken Starr and Henry Hyde got in the mud first. I just decided to jump in there with them." Then Bob Livingston on the House floor, December 19, 1998.

The ad ran October 4, 1998. Flynt told Time he got more than 2,000 calls.

On December 17, Livingston told Republican colleagues he had "on occasion strayed from my marriage." He began with: "I guess I have been Larry Flynted." Flynt said Hustler had been working on tips about four women. "Frankly, we were getting ready to go with this story and are disappointed he scooped us."

Two days later Livingston told Clinton from the floor: "You, sir, may resign your post." Democrats shouted back, "You resign!" Then he did. "So I must set the example that I hope President Clinton will follow," he said, and thanked his wife "for standing by me."

That night he told the Los Angeles Times: "The president's actions were a breach of the public's trust. My actions were a breach of my wife's trust." Days later Flynt said Bonnie Livingston had asked him not to publish. "He's resigned, what's the point?"

The case for Flynt: the next Speaker of a House impeaching a president for lying about an affair had affairs too, and admitted it. The case against him: he put a price on private lives, and by his own account he only paused when Livingston's wife contacted him.

Was Larry Flynt exposing hypocrites, or buying their secrets?

text:
A Just War in Half Measures

The autopsy of the Republican collapse in the midterm elections was delivered with indecent haste and familiar indolence. Across the transatlantic commentary class, the consensus was minted within hours: Donald Trump’s Iranian venture had throttled the Strait of Hormuz, sent the price of crude soaring, and driven a combustible electorate to mutiny at the ballot box. It is a neat, comforting narrative, and largely superficial. The American electorate’s weariness with Trump is chronic and omnivorous, spanning the chaotic theatre of his domestic agenda and the erratic choreography of his diplomacy. The Iranian campaign was not the sole author of his misfortune, nor even its primary architect.

Measured against the swamp of Vietnam or the generational quagmire of Afghanistan, this campaign has demanded neither the blood nor the treasure of its catastrophic predecessors. There were no tens of thousands in the streets chanting against the war machine; the public’s true grievance was far more banal. They did not despise the strike; they detested the ensuing, indecisive drift—a president who possessed the audacity to kick open the hornets' nest, yet lacked the institutional appetite to burn it to the ground.

Let us dispense with the polite fictions of international etiquette: Trump was right to wage this war. The theocracy in Tehran has long constituted one of the modern world’s most unredeemed despotic projects—the central clearing-house and spiritual bankroller of Islamist terror, an enduring engine of regional extortion. To have suffered its continued existence unchallenged was simply to subsidise global insecurity on the instalment plan.

The enterprise unfolded across two deliberate movements. The first, in late June 2025, saw American ordnance obliterate three of the regime’s crown-jewel nuclear subterranean sites with bunker-busting finality. Tehran had hauled its enrichment toward the 90 per cent weapons-grade threshold, leaving the civilized world mere weeks—perhaps days—from a nuclear fait accompli. One scarcely needs to rehearse what a nuclear-armed clerical dictatorship would have meant: a global economy held permanently hostage to apocalyptic blackmail, granting the mullahs licence to run amok across the Middle East with absolute impunity.

The second act, launched this past February under the grandiose rubrics of Epic Fury and Roaring Lion, exploited Israeli intelligence with lethal precision. Striking a conclave of the regime’s high command, the blitz decapitated more than fifty senior figures, including Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei himself. With the Iranian street already roiling in open rebellion and the state machinery visibly trembling, the blow was designed to induce terminal systemic collapse.

That it failed to do so is a testament to the stubborn resilience of ideological tyranny. Defying Western expectations, the clerical apparat endured the slaughter, absorbed the shock, and gradually reasserted its domestic stranglehold while snarling defiance abroad. A strategic disappointment, certainly, but an operational stall does not retrospectively invalidate the moral premise of the war.

A regime that butchers its own people within and manufactures terror abroad forfeits any moral title to sovereignty. The customary invocation of "non-intervention" is a doctrine intended for civilised neighbours in an orderly cul-de-sac. Observance of international rules requires reciprocity; to adhere rigidly to Marquess of Queensberry courtesies while your adversary brandishes a shiv is not noble statecraft, but pure, unadulterated imbecility.

The United Nations, conceived in the post-war glow of American triumph, has long since degenerated into a toothless circus. Suborned by Beijing’s ledger-book imperialism and paralysed by Moscow’s cynical obstruction, the institution has witnessed the disenfranchisement of Western democracies. When the revisionist rogue’s gallery—China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran—regard international law as a disposable fiction, unilateral piety on the part of the West is an act of strategic suicide.

Yet the campaign now languishes in an excruciating holding pattern. Dreading the casualty lists of a ground invasion, Washington opted for immaculate remote warfare, leaving itself open to Tehran’s asymmetric chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. The result is the dreary spectacle of fighting while talking, a protracted war of diplomatic inches.

The debit column is plain enough: an inflated defence ledger, erratic spikes at the petrol pump, and shipping lanes choked with tension. But the strategic ledger tells another story. The nuclear peril has been dismantled, at least for a generation; the regime’s domestic aura of invulnerability has been pulverized, its armed forces shattered beyond near-term repair. Whatever fragile armistice eventually emerges, Tehran’s capacity to menace the globe has been decisively gutted. Its axis partners in Beijing, Moscow, and Pyongyang, having offered copious rhetoric and moral solidarity, were ultimately reduced to spectators, watching their regional satrapy systematically defanged.

Stripped of theatrical excess, the campaign served fundamental Western interests. To permit a messianic regime to acquire the bomb whilst chanting "Death to America" would have been negligence bordering on treason. Striking the head of the serpent was the only coherent leverage to give the Iranian people a fighting chance at emancipation. Any American commander-in-chief, regardless of partisan label, presented with such intelligence, had an existential duty to pull the trigger.

The paradox of modern democracy, however, is that it wills the victory while abhorring the cost. Had the Pentagon committed the full weight of its land forces, the conventional regime would have been crushed like brittle porcelain. But ground wars extract blood, and democratic electorates are notoriously allergic to body bags. Caught between the strategic necessity of decisive force and the electoral peril of a long casualty roll, Trump hesitated—and in that hesitation, the initiative slipped away.

Western societies demand cheap petrol, undisturbed domestic serenity, and untarnished moral clean hands, all while the barbarians bang on the city gates. It is an infantile delusion. The relative peace and democratic luxury the West has inherited was not bartered across mahogany tables; it was purchased in the charnel houses of the twentieth century by generations who understood that evil must occasionally be liquidated, not endlessly managed.

Trump was entirely justified in striking Tehran, just as he was right to run Nicolás Maduro out of Caracas. Civilisation inches forward only when free nations occasionally remind the world’s thugs that their leases are revocable. The alternative is the perpetual, dignified retreat of the appeaser: endless conferences, sternly worded communiqués, and humiliating compromise, until the fight is brought to our own doorsteps on vastly worse terms. If the West has forgotten how to finish the wars it rightfully starts, it has only its own faint-hearted vanity to thank.

🥩 America’s $100 Billion Beef Industry Faces Major Downsizing as High Meat Prices Threaten to Become Permanent

🐄 America’s Cattle Herd Is Shrinking: The U.S. beef industry is facing a prolonged supply crisis as years of drought, rising production costs, and declining cattle numbers force ranchers to reduce their herds. With fewer animals available for slaughter, beef supplies are tightening, putting continued upward pressure on prices at grocery stores and restaurants.

💰 Consumers Face Persistently High Prices: Americans are paying more for steaks, ground beef, and other popular cuts as cattle shortages collide with strong consumer demand. Even if inflation slows elsewhere in the economy, beef prices could remain elevated because rebuilding the nation's cattle supply takes years.

🏭 Meatpacking Industry Under Pressure: Large meat processors face tighter supplies of slaughter ready cattle, increasing competition for livestock and squeezing profit margins. Processing plants built to handle larger herds may be forced to reduce production, cut jobs, or close facilities as the industry adjusts to fewer available animals.

📉 Cattle Population Hits a 75 Year Low: America's cattle herd has fallen to approximately 86 million animals, its smallest population since the early 1950s. Ground beef prices have increased by nearly 57% over five years, illustrating how severely the shortage has affected household food budgets.

🚜 Ranchers Cannot Rebuild Overnight: Even with cattle prices reaching record levels, expanding herds remains difficult. Ranchers must retain breeding females instead of selling them, wait for calves to be born, and raise those animals to market weight. The entire process can take several years, meaning meaningful supply improvements may not arrive until the end of the decade.

🌎 Imports Offer Limited Relief: Federal efforts to increase foreign beef imports could ease some shortages, particularly for ground beef. However, imported meat cannot immediately replace the millions of cattle missing from American ranches, limiting how quickly consumers could see substantial price reductions.

⏳ High Beef Prices Could Persist Into the 2030s: The combination of historically low cattle inventories, shrinking processing capacity, expensive ranching operations, and strong demand threatens to keep beef prices elevated well into the next decade. While prices may fluctuate, a sustained return to previous levels is increasingly difficult without a significant recovery in domestic cattle production.

text:
Socialism just took another deliberate step forward in New York City on Tuesday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA) and said it’ll “give New Yorkers a tool to keep their homes out of the hands of predatory investors seeking to make a quick and easy buck.” That framing’s the tell. It treats private owners who want to sell on the open market as the problem and government-approved nonprofits as the solution. This is how socialists advance. They restrict the right to sell property, insert a preferred-buyer list, and call the restriction protection.

The bill gives qualified nonprofits, land trusts, and community groups first rights to buy certain multifamily buildings before they hit the open market. Capitalism depends on owners being able to transfer property freely. COPA replaces that with a mandatory delay and a government-vetted list of buyers. The market’s no longer first.

Mamdani’s long described the goal as “decommodifying” housing. That’s the socialist position: housing stops being something people buy and sell on the open market and becomes something allocated by approved nonprofits and the city. The law operationalizes that idea one category of buildings at a time. Sponsored by Council Member Sandy Nurse, it targets properties with four or more units that meet distress criteria. Qualified groups get an exclusive window to offer and a later right of first refusal. It takes effect in November 2027.

Other cities have tested versions of this. Washington, D.C.’s long-running Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act delayed sales by an average of five months, reduced transaction volume relative to neighboring jurisdictions, and left some buildings with owners who wanted out but couldn’t sell efficiently. The District rolled the law back in 2025 after describing “significant financial distress.” San Francisco’s COPA has preserved a few hundred units, but only with substantial public subsidies and on a limited scale.

The City Council passed the narrowed bill 38-9 in October after Adams vetoed an earlier version. Mamdani made it a priority in his housing plan and signed it immediately. Property owners of eligible buildings now face a preferred-buyer process designed by the same administration that’s already failed to lower rents or everyday costs. Median asking rent hit a record under him. This law adds another layer of control on top of that record.

When the preferred-buyer process and mandatory delays reduce what an owner can realistically get for a building, private capital leaves. Investors put money into markets where they can sell freely and get the full price. The buildings that stay under the restricted system get less maintenance, less new supply, and more reliance on city subsidies. That’s the collapse path. D.C. already started down it and had to roll its law back. New York just chose the same experiment as if somehow the results will differ. They won’t. The incentives don’t change.

Spartz’s office has also disputed aspects of West’s account of her employment and termination.

text:
@HiThere144 I hike the Appalachians, Tennessee and Kentucky, frequently. Not a pro — just someone who enjoys hiking. And I like boots and shoes. 😂

Steel-soled boots? I’ve never seen them. Logically, I think they’d be impractical and dangerous for distance hiking — too heavy, slippery, stiff, and they conduct temperature; however, I am now intrigued. Do you own boots with an entire steel sole? Or are you perhaps describing steel toe, steel shank, or steel midsole? 

I’m curious, now, from your statement and knowledge - so I’m explaining what I do know (or think I know 😂), and maybe learn something new from you that I don’t know (and didn’t even know I didn’t know it). 😊 So, feel free to correct me and please share your knowledge. I’ve hiked some in the western states, by far the most in Colorado, but a few other states at one point - not extensively by any means. 

Steel toe protects against crushing in work settings and offers some toe protection on rough rock, but the weight outweighs any benefit for hikers. I own Ariat steel-toed and Keen hybrid work/hiking boots — both far too heavy for trails.

Steel-shanked boots provide support and weight distribution useful for carrying heavy loads on job sites. Overkill for distance hiking. Hikers who want that structure go for lighter materials — nylon, polycarbonate, carbon fiber. 

Steel-reinforced midsoles matter around nails and glass shards. Rarely chosen for hiking, and if someone did want that protection, newer composites give the same benefit at a fraction of the weight.

Steel is heavy, rigid, non-breathable, and temperature-conductive. It’s increasingly replaced by carbon fiber, Kevlar, or lightweight metals. There may be work conditions where steel wins, but experienced hikers almost never pick it.

From both my experience and knowledge, trail runners or ultralight boots are preferred by most hikers — lightweight, breathable, flexible, quick-drying, with grip for rock, roots, dirt, wet places, even desert sand. Trail runners for a light pack, ultralight boots for a heavier one, and some switch between the two along the way.

Of course, some hikers have a penchant for a particular shoe. Emma “Grandma” Gatewood, who in 1955 at 67 years old was the first woman to solo hike the entire AT, wore canvas Keds sneakers. 

Hiking footwear costs too much to toss after one trip — you wear it until it no longer functions. Broken-in is much better than new to be honest, because blisters are the number one reason people quit the AT. I’ve seen some of those. OUCH!!

"Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever!"

These were the words of Hakeem Jeffries, who is today the leading candidate to become Speaker of the US House of Representatives, at a pro-Israel rally in 2014. He offered this performance at the very height of Israel's murderous assault on the Gaza Strip of that year.

Jeffries, who is African-American, knowingly parroted the 1963 proclamation by the arch-segregationist and Alabama Governor George Wallace: "Segregation now, segregation tomorrow, segregation forever!" 

It is of course entirely fitting that Jeffries invoked the slogan of Jim Crow's defiant last stand to demonstrate his fealty to Israel's apartheid regime.

At the time Jeffries's repulsive sloganeering passed largely without comment, apart from fulsome praise. 

Had Jeffries made a similar statement about any other foreign state, even a close US ally like Great Britain or Poland, he would have instantly been accused of treason. As would any politician anywhere else making such explicit statements of loyalty to a foreign state.

Yet for Israel there has always been an exception, an exemption from the rules.

This is now slowly but surely coming to an end, and may even cost Jeffries the coveted House leadership position.

Running for office makes blanket denials the expected and rational response for self-preservation, regardless of the underlying facts. The usable basis is therefore the documented pattern of associations, signed statements, and family statements that have been reported across multiple outlets.

What is documented

Half-sister Eman Abdelhadi’s own posts (2012–2013): She stated “My family has long been MB,” described her mother’s activism in the Muslim Brotherhood while in college in Egypt in the early 1970s (adding “#respect”), referred to relatives jailed for MB involvement, and prayed for family members supporting the group. These are her words, not third-party speculation. The campaign has said El-Sayed loves his sister but disagrees with her on various political positions and rhetoric.⁠

2012 letter El-Sayed signed: As a Columbia medical student he was one of 46 signatories on an Arabic statement (published in Al-Ahram Gate) supporting Mohamed Morsi’s “revolutionary decisions” and calling on him to “purge the media and the police as quickly as possible.” Morsi was the Muslim Brotherhood’s political standard-bearer. The New York Times and others confirmed the signature; El-Sayed has not offered a detailed public explanation and has broadly denied MB ties. Some reporting notes the letter itself did not name the Brotherhood and can be read as support for post-Mubarak institutional change.

Mother Fatten Elkomy’s employment: She worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA-USA) roughly 1999–2004. The broader network was later designated by the U.S. Treasury for providing financial support linked to al-Qaeda, Hamas, and the Taliban. Court exhibits reference her involvement in transfers (including orphan-related). She was never charged or named as a defendant; the campaign states she was helping orphaned children. The FBI interviewed her after the 2004 designation/raid.⁠

Wife’s family: Father-in-law Tayeb Jukaku has long been involved with the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA founding committee) and CAIR Michigan (former chapter president, current board). Both organizations have documented historical connections to Muslim Brotherhood networks in the United States (including material from the Holy Land Foundation trial). A sister-in-law was placed on a terrorism watchlist and participated in CAIR-backed litigation over it. The family’s Indian roots (Karnataka/Bhatkal) are otherwise described in ordinary political and professional terms.⁠

El-Sayed’s own public record: Consistently strong anti-Israel positions and associations with figures such as Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur (whose rhetoric frequently collapses Israel/Zionism into broader Jewish or “Jewish supremacy” framing). He has denied personal antisemitism and framed his stance as opposition to Israeli policy. 

I am not sure how much noise needs to be around a candidate for the electors to come to a common sense, sensible judgement – but then perhaps it is all about "#SuicidalEmpathy"

text:
Most days in her chambers, Judge Maritza Braswell, a federal magistrate judge in Colorado, sifts through stacks of documents written by people without a lawyer. Many of them can’t afford to hire a lawyer, and others have cases too weak or too small to interest one. She reads each one carefully, mindful of how daunting it is to walk into the courtroom alone. 

Lately, like many judges across the US, she has seen a noticeable uptick in such filings. According to a new study that examined 4.5 million federal civil cases from 2005 to 2026, the share of lawsuits brought by self-represented people increased from 11% in 2022 to 16.8% in 2025. Within those cases, the number of filings made more than doubled from pre-2023 levels. 

Judge Braswell puts that jump down to AI. 

“I do correlate that to AI in part because I see AI use,” she says. As a tech-savvy judge who uses AI to vet court documents, she’s learned to recognize how large language models write. She can tell from the prose and at times, hallucinated cases and fabricated quotes. 

“I’m also actually seeing better-drafted pleadings,” she says. 

But while AI appears to be expanding access to justice, it doesn’t seem to be improving people’s chances of winning. Judges are also starting to question what kinds of rights and responsibilities large language models should bear as they step into lawyers’ shoes. For example, they ask whether a chatbot has a duty to provide good advice, as a human lawyer does. And a growing number of lawmakers across the US are starting to grapple with who should pay the price when chatbots dish out bad legal advice. 


AI supercharges lawsuits

To test whether AI was driving the increase in lawsuits filed by people without a lawyer, the authors of the study, Anand Shah at MIT and Joshua Levy at the University of Southern California, ran 1,600 randomly sampled court documents through Pangram, a commercial AI-text detector. The share flagged as containing AI-generated writing rose from 1% in 2023 to 18% in 2026. 

To Judge Braswell, that’s not necessarily a cause for concern. While the surge of AI-assisted filings might be adding to their workloads, she and many other judges find the cases easier to rule on because AI is helping people without legal training better articulate their arguments. 

Court documents written by people without lawyers are notoriously hard to decipher. Some arrive as handwritten scrawls bordering on gibberish that judges take a while to decode. However cryptic, judges are required to read them charitably.

These days, Judge Braswell has been churning through motions drafted by AI faster than the ones written by the litigants. “I have to be really careful because some of them contain hallucinations and errors, but I can generally understand what they’re arguing better with AI assistance from them than without it,” she says.

The clearer filings let Judge Braswell hear them better. “If I understand an argument a little bit better, I’m probably going to be able to help a little bit more,” she says.

Online communities are springing up to trade self-help guides on using AI to sue. In December 2024, a viral Reddit post walked immigration applicants through suing the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services over delayed review of their applications: draft a writ of mandamus with Microsoft Copilot, pay a lawyer $150 to polish it, and file in the expedient District of Vermont. Cases filed by people without lawyers in Vermont rose from about 45 a year before 2022 to more than 1,100 in 2024. 

Even so, people without lawyers are far more likely to lose their case than people with lawyers, and that’s not changing even with the addition of AI, the study found. 

“It turns out that mounting a lawsuit is a complex, multifaceted task. Not all of it is just drafting text,” says Levy. 

Chatbot-client privilege

Judge William Garfinkel, a federal magistrate judge in Connecticut, has served on the bench for three decades, pondering all sorts of questions about lawyers’ relationship with their clients. Lately, he has been wondering whether people’s conversations with chatbots dispensing legal advice should be privileged, the way their conversations with lawyers are. 

“You can make a good argument that … conversations with large language models like Claude or ChatGPT or Grok should deserve some protection,” he says.

Courts are starting to grapple with this question. In February, a federal court in Michigan ruled that a self-represented person’s conversations with ChatGPT to prepare her case were work product—legal work that is shielded from the opposing side.

The decision came on the same day a federal court in New York held that documents a criminal defendant had generated using Claude were not privileged attorney-client conversations or work product. The court argued that Claude is not an attorney and that a user has no “reasonable expectation of confidentiality in his communication” with it because AI companies can disclose user data to third parties. 

In March, Judge Braswell ruled that a self-represented person’s use of a chatbot should stay off limits. “It is true that AI systems like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and others … collect user data for training and other purposes. But … that does not eliminate all expectations of privacy,” she wrote. Courts have since remained split on the issue.

Malpractice without a pulse

Some judges are also wondering whether a chatbot, like a lawyer, has a duty to provide good legal advice. Judge Allison Goddard, a federal magistrate judge in California, has noticed that people without lawyers often get the wrong advice from ChatGPT when trying to assess the value of their case during settlement negotiations. In one case, a plaintiff who slipped and fell in a store asked for $700,000 from the store, which was wildly more than the case was worth.

“Where are you getting the idea that you’re getting $700,000? Did you go to ChatGPT?” Judge Goddard asked. “Well …” the plaintiff mumbled. She then walked the person through the law to explain why ChatGPT was wrong and suggested a lower amount. “It’s like Dr. Google went to law school,” she says.

Then there’s the question of who’s liable when a chatbot makes such mistakes. In March, Nippon Life Insurance Company sued OpenAI alleging that ChatGPT practiced law without a license and helped a woman reopen a lawsuit that was already settled, flooding the court with frivolous filings. “ChatGPT is not an attorney,” the lawsuit said. 

In May, OpenAI asked the court to dismiss the case, arguing that ChatGPT does not practice law. “ChatGPT is not a person and neither has nor uses any degree of legal ​knowledge or skill,” OpenAI said in its filing. The case is still pending before the court.

States have started to weigh legislation that would hold AI companies liable when their chatbots offer bad legal advice. New York introduced a bill in March that would bar chatbots from impersonating lawyers, even if they notify ​users that they are interacting with chatbots. In Congress, a series of bills have been proposed to ban chatbots from posing as lawyers, doctors, and other licensed professionals. The bills have yet to gain traction.

For now, people will continue turning to AI to be their lawyer. For many of them, the rewards outweigh the risks. Not long ago, when Judge Braswell asked self-represented litigants why they wanted a particular piece of evidence, they mumbled timidly. Now, they answer her questions confidently, having rehearsed with a chatbot. 

“This is a really tough system to navigate. With AI, though, it gets a little less complex,” she says.

At least 11 states are providing additional help with Affordable Care Act insurance premiums for 2027, with Rhode Island and Virginia launching new programs as households continue adjusting to the loss of enhanced federal subsidies.

The other states are California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Mexico, New Jersey, Vermont and Washington. Their assistance supplements the regular federal premium tax credits that remain available to eligible marketplace enrollees.

The enhanced federal credits expired at the end of 2025. Benzinga cited KFF findings that average monthly premium payments increased 58% in 2026, reaching $178 from $113. Federal figures also showed enrollment falling to 19.2 million in February 2026 from 22.1 million a year earlier.

California is increasing its state subsidy funding to $300 million for 2027, up from $190 million. Eligibility expands to households earning up to 200% of the federal poverty level, making approximately 200,000 additional people eligible for help.

Covered California says the expanded program is projected to benefit more than 500,000 residents, roughly 30% of its enrollees. The agency also cautions that state funding cannot replace the nearly $2.5 billion Californians previously received annually through enhanced federal credits.

The state programs offer meaningful assistance, but the amount of relief depends on where people live and whether they qualify. As 2027 enrollment proceeds, the central issue is how much of the higher insurance bill state budgets can absorb.
